According to recent reports, the structure of the PseCAST holocomplex reveals the molecular interactions responsible for the TnsC-dependent recruitment of TnsAB to the target DNA to effect site-specific donor integration. The TnsB.1 subunit is tethered to the C-terminal face of the TnsC heptamer by its β-barrel domain (residues 434–500), positioned at the interface of the TnsC.1 and TnsC.7 subunits (Fig. 3e). TnsC.1 inserts its C-terminal loop—spanning residues 314–322 and including Leu318—into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Val472, Gln467 and Leu441 in the TnsB.1 β-barrel domain (Fig. 3e). In turn, Asn316 of TnsC, situated in the same loop in TnsC.7, interacts through hydrogen bonds with Arg443 and Asn444 in TnsB.1 (Fig. 3e). Aspartate substitutions of Leu318 in TnsC (L318D) or Val472 in TnsB (V472D) resulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 3f). The single TnsC mutation N316A or replacement of TnsC loop residues 316–321 with a (Gly–Ser)3 linker resulted in modestly impaired activity. By contrast, the single TnsB mutations R443E or N444D strongly reduced transposition activity (Fig. 3f), confirming that the formation of this interface is essential for PseCAST-mediated DNA transposition.

In addition to interactions with TnsC, the β-barrel domain of the catalytic TnsB.1 subunit also interacts with the backbone of the target DNA segment downstream of the TnsC heptamer, forming a network of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic contacts using Arg439, Thr440, Lys447 and Gln449 of TnsB (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, Lys520 and Arg524 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB also contact the target DNA backbone. Notably, this domain adopts a helical bundle fold that bridges the catalytic and β-barrel domains in the catalytic TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits. By contrast, the helical domain of the structural TnsB.3 and TnsB.4 subunits forms two stretched helices that are sandwiched between the catalytic domain and DNA-binding domain 2 of TnsAB.1 and TnsAB.2, contributing to intra-subunit contacts.

Together, these insights highlight the functional role of the TnsB β-barrel domain in transpososome assembly. The shape complementarity of the TnsC and TnsB β-barrel interaction surfaces, together with cooperative interactions with the target DNA, provide the structural basis for the molecular ruler mechanism that defines the integration site, enabling the transposon to be inserted at a fixed distance of 49 nucleotides from the crRNA-specified target site. Moreover, the synergistic contacts with two TnsC subunits and the target DNA underlie a checkpoint mechanism that senses target DNA-dependent TnsC oligomerization, thereby explaining the strictly sequential assembly of the transpososome observed in type I-F systems40.

The structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex captures the TnsAB STC tetramer in a post-integration state (Fig. 4a,b). As in the PEC structure45, the active sites of the TnsA.1 and TnsA.2 subunits interact with the 5′ termini of the transposon ends, adopting a catalytically competent, post-cleavage geometry in which the catalytic triad residues Glu34, Asp71 and Lys87 of TnsA coordinate the 5′-terminal phosphate group and a single Mg2+ ion (Fig. 4c). In contrast to the PEC structure, the catalytic sites of the TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits also assume an activated conformation in which a Mg2+ ion—coordinated by the catalytic triad residues Asp220, Asp304 and Glu340 of TnsB—interacts with the 3′-hydroxyl group of the terminal nucleotide (dG76 in the NTGS) of the target DNA and the phosphodiester group that links the TSD segment to the 3′-terminal nucleotide of the transposon end (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, the catalytic domain establishes contacts with RE and TSD nucleotides that are crucial for STC formation (Fig. 4d). Specifically, Asp225 of TnsB positions an additional Mg2+ ion such that it simultaneously coordinates the phosphate groups of dA(−82) and dG(−80), stabilizing a kink in the DNA backbone at the TSD–RE junction that enables STC formation. The backbone is additionally contacted by Thr222, Arg239 and Ser360 of TnsB (Fig. 4d). Consistent with these observations, alanine substitution of Asp225 (D225A) or a charge-reversal mutation of Arg239 of TnsB (R239E) resulted in a complete loss of PseCAST transposition activity in E. coli, whereas TnsB mutations T222A or S360A only reduced PseCAST activity (Fig. 4e).

In a recent development, a, Schematic of the TnsAB STC. BB, β-barrel domain; ENDO, endonuclease domain; HD, helical domain; HEL CTD, helical C-terminal domain. b, Structures of TnsAB bound to DNA (grey) in the STC state in the PseCAST holocomplex (left) and in the PEC (right) conformations. TnsB domains that become structured in the STC are indicated. c, Magnification of the 5′-terminal transposon-end overhang in the catalytic site of TnsA. d, Magnification of the TnsB catalytic site and interactions between the TSD DNA and the TnsB catalytic domain. e, RNA-guided transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST systems containing mutations in the TnsB residues involved in contacting the TSD region of the target DNA, as quantified by qPCR. f, Magnification of the interface between the β-barrel, C-terminal helical domain, C-terminal tail and catalytic domains of TnsB in the STC. g,h, Magnifications of the structural overlays of TnsAB in the PEC (blue) and STC (orange) states. g, Allosteric remodelling of the TnsB catalytic domain, ordering of the region comprising TnsB residues 346–369 and shift in the helix containing the catalytic residue Glu340 of TnsB. h, Ordering of the first 12 N-terminal residues of TnsA. i, RNA-guided transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST systems containing mutations in the N-terminus of TnsA and in the residues at the interface shown in f, as quantified by qPCR. e,i, Data are mean ± s.d. of three biologically independent replicates (n = 3; circles); TnsB mutation D220A serves as a negative control.

It has been revealed that finally, the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex structure highlights a potential allosteric relay mechanism that underlies the target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB. In the PEC structure, the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the catalytic TnsB subunits are disordered45. By contrast, both domains are structured in the STC state and interface with the catalytic domain (Fig. 4b) through a network of hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions (Fig. 4f). This is coupled with local structural remodelling of the catalytic domain, resulting in the ordering of an adjacent loop (residues Glu348–Lys369 of TnsB) (Fig. 4g) and an approximately 11-Å concomitant shift of the helix bearing the catalytic Glu340 residue of TnsB (Fig. 4g). The conformational rearrangement marks the transition of the catalytic site from an inactive, post-excision state to an active, strand-transfer configuration that supports Mg2+ coordination and catalytic activity. Consistent with these observations, combined alanine substitutions of Lys567, Gln571 and Asn577 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB strongly reduced the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli (Fig. 4i). Additional ordering was observed for the N-terminal segment (residues Met1–Pro11) of the TnsA helical domain, which positions the Arg4 residue of TnsA such that it contacts the 5′-terminal phosphate of the cleaved transposon end (Fig. 4c,h), implicating TnsA in TnsB activation. Accordingly, truncation of the TnsA N-terminal segment (ΔMet1–Asn12) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 4i). Together, the structural observations and their functional validation indicate that the molecular interfaces formed between the C-terminal, β-barrel and catalytic domains of TnsB after binding to the target DNA and TnsC are required to support the integration activity of PseCAST. Both target DNA and TnsC synergistically couple transposase recruitment with domain ordering and catalytic-site remodelling, resulting in the allosteric activation of TnsB for site-specific DNA integration.

Our structural and functional analyses of the PseCAST system comprehensively revealed the molecular mechanism that underlies RNA-guided transposon integration by type I-F CASTs, in which an orchestrated series of interactions and conformational rearrangements couples target recognition with site-specific DNA insertion. Together, these insights support a mechanistic model in which DNA transposition is controlled by a succession of molecular checkpoints (Fig. 5). The formation of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex requires R-loop completion, enabled by a conformational rearrangement of the Cas8 subunit, including the approximately 90° rotation of the helical bundle domain into a locked conformation. In contrast to the open conformations reported previously for type I-F CAST QCascade complexes9,19,21,37, this locked state positions the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex for binding to TniQ, which facilitates ATP-dependent TnsC assembly on the target DNA by interacting with Cas8 and TniQ. As the locked Cas8 conformation is achieved only with fully matched targets, it acts as a fidelity checkpoint that discriminates against mismatched sites, underpinning the high target specificity of PseCAST. Instead of forming extended filaments as in type V CASTs32,33, PseTnsC assembles into a symmetric heptamer to fully encircle the DNA duplex exiting QCascade. The transposon insertion site is thus defined by the physical footprint and register of the TnsC ring, rather than by TnsB-dependent TnsC depolymerization6,32,33. The initial recruitment of the TnsAB transposase PEC is mediated by the TnsB C-terminal tail hook motifs. As these interactions are dependent on TnsC heptamerization, this step provides another fidelity checkpoint that makes transposition dependent on the correct recognition of the DNA target. Finally, productive target engagement by TnsAB requires conformational ordering of the TnsB β-barrel domain and C-terminal helices, driven by interactions of the TnsB β-barrel domain with the target DNA and the TnsC heptamer. This is coupled with structural remodelling of the TnsB active site into a catalytically competent configuration. Therefore, the TnsC- and target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB acts as a final fidelity checkpoint, ensuring that transposon DNA insertion proceeds only once the transposase is correctly anchored to the target DNA. Together, our findings reveal the structural coupling of target DNA engagement and transposase activation, but the precise role of allosteric interactions in the observed conformational rearrangements requires further investigation. We speculate that similar structural coupling is involved in activating TnsAB for transposon excision after interacting with the flanking segments of the donor DNA.

According to recent reports, the Cascade–TniQ complex is guided to the target DNA by base-pairing with its crRNA, leading to the initial formation of a partial R-loop. Coordination of the displaced NTGS by the Cas8 helical bundle is coupled with the transition of the bundle from open to closed, full R-loop formation and the stabilization of the double-stranded PAM-distal target-DNA duplex by the TniQ dimer. TnsC is recruited to the target site, where it assembles into a closed heptameric ring by binding to the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex in the presence of ATP, TniQ and Cas8. At the donor site, excision of the transposon DNA by TnsAB involves the formation of a PEC. The PEC is initially recruited by the TnsC heptamer by interacting with the C-terminal TnsB hooks. Interactions with the target DNA and TnsC result in structural remodelling of the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the interfacing TnsB copies, which is allosterically coupled with a conformational rearrangement of the catalytic domains into an active conformation (the asterisks indicate active TnsB sites). The transposon DNA is integrated by two transesterification reactions catalysed by the active sites of the interfacing TnsBs, covalently linking both transposon 3′ ends to the target DNA with 5-base-pair spacing that results in a target-site duplication (TSD).

Directed evolution and structure-guided engineering are powerful complementary strategies for improving CAST activity8,9, recalling previous studies in which structural insights have enabled the rational design of hyperactive variants of the Sleeping Beauty transposase50,51. To provide a structural context for current engineering efforts, we mapped the activity-enhancing substitutions of evoCAST onto the PseCAST holocomplex structure (Extended Data Fig. 9). Two of these, F43S in TnsB and P88T in TnsA, have already been interpreted structurally in the PseTnsAB PEC as potentially facilitating transposon end recognition and stabilizing the cleaved NTGS overhang, respectively. Several of the remaining substitutions in TnsB, which were mostly unresolved in the PEC, can now be interpreted. Y349N, P352T and D396N are found close to the target-DNA substrate, potentially enhancing its binding. Q410K, V526E and Q549R are predominantly surface-facing and thus likely to enhance protein solubility or stability. Q594L, although unresolved in the holocomplex structure, may provide additional hydrophobic interactions to the interface formed between the C-terminal hook and TnsC, which is essential for transposase recruitment. Finally, H464R may promote the interaction between the TnsB β-barrel domain and TnsC through enhanced electrostatic contacts. The substitutions R197I and N314K in TnsC map to the TnsC oligomerization interface and the TnsC–TnsB interface, respectively. Lastly, in addition to the PAM-enhancing mutations N125D and A244N in Cas8, the A410R substitution in the helical bundle likely contacts the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex after R-loop completion (Fig. 5), potentially stabilizing the locked QCascade conformation and promoting TnsC assembly. Together, these insights suggest that evoCAST activity results from the synergistic optimization of DNA binding, intersubunit contacts, folding and solubility. Therefore, future engineering efforts should continue to use both structure-guided and directed-evolution approaches.

In conclusion, the structural findings presented here reveal the molecular mechanisms underpinning RNA-guided transposition by type I CASTs, providing a framework for their further rational engineering for technological applications.

The expression plasmids containing His10–TEV-tagged TniQ and Cas8 (pSL4521), Cas7, Cas6 and the CRISPR array (pSL4522), His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsC (pSL5536) and His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsAB fusion protein (pSL3768) were cloned using standard molecular biology methods including Gibson52 and Golden Gate53 assembly. All plasmids were sequence-verified using whole-plasmid Nanopore sequencing (Genewiz). To clone the expression plasmid containing Cas7, the CRISPR array and Twin-Strep-tagged Cas6 (pMS321), a Twin-Strep-tag54 was added to the C-terminus of cas6 by Gibson assembly: pSL4522 was linearized by PCR using oMS603 and oMS604, and the Twin-Strep-tag was amplified by PCR from a common backbone using the primers oMS605 and oMS606, which contain overhangs compatible with the linearized pSL4522 plasmid. Constructs for expression of His6–MBP-tagged versions of the TnsAB fusion protein and TnsB were generated by PCR amplification of the coding sequence using pSL3768 as template and primer pairs oMS631-632 and oMS634-632, respectively. The PCR products were inserted in the 1C backbone (Addgene; 29654) by ligation-independent cloning55. The His6–MBP-tagged TnsB C-terminal tail (residues 575–613) was prepared by Gibson assembly, using the His6–MBP–TnsB plasmid as a template and the primer pairs oGF181-182 and oGF180-184 to generate the PCR fragments. Plasmids were cloned and propagated in Mach I cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), purified using the GeneJET plasmid miniprep kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and verified by full-plasmid sequencing or Sanger sequencing (Microsynth). All sequences of primers and parental plasmids used for cloning are provided in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

In a recent development, for Cascade–TniQ protein expression, the plasmid pSL4521 encoding His10–TEV–TniQ and Cas8 and the plasmid pMS321 encoding Cas7, Cas6–Twin-Strep and the crRNA were transformed together in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Rosetta2 (DE3) cells (Novagen), plated on an agar plate and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of Luria broth (LB) to obtain a starter culture. Both the transformation plate and liquid medium were supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 50 µg ml−1 streptomycin and 33 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing antibiotic-supplemented (kanamycin, streptomycin) LB medium to reach a starting optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.4 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min) and resuspended in 100 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin and 200 μg ml−1 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride (AEBSF). The suspension was lysed using a Maximator cell homogenizer at 1,500 bar and 4 °C. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 40 min) and applied to three 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 200 ml of HisTrap wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) and eluted with 50 ml of HisTrap elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole). Dithiothreitol (DTT) and ATP were added to the eluted sample to a final concentration of 1 mM each. The sample was added to 7 ml of 50% Strep-Tactin affinity resin suspension (IBA Lifesciences) in HisTrap elution buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 30 min. The protein-bound resin was washed with 70 ml of size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT) and the sample was eluted with 20 ml of SEC buffer supplemented with 5 mM d-desthiobiotin. Eluted fractions were further purified by SEC using a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) column in SEC buffer. Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 10 mg ml−1 using a 30-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

Recent findings suggest that for TnsC expression, the vector pSL5536 encoding His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was transformed in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), plated on an agar plate supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of kanamycin-supplemented LB to obtain a starter culture. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing kanamycin-supplemented LB medium to reach a starting OD600 of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.3 mM IPTG for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min). Proteins were purified as described previously for the TnsC of Vibrio cholerae40. A cell pellet (corresponding to four 750-ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5 mM magnesium acetate, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 20% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000 g at 4 °C for 45 min) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 10 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). The columns were washed with 90 ml of equilibration buffer and 50 ml of wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 30 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT), and the proteins were eluted with 10 ml of elution buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 300 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). Elution fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 10 mM imidazole) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Any precipitated protein was removed by centrifugation (20,000g at 4 °C for 20 min). The dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer. The columns were washed with 60 ml of equilibration buffer, 90 ml of wash buffer and 50 ml of elution buffer. Flowthrough and initial wash fractions were applied to a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 12 mg ml−1 using a 10-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

For the expression of His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsAB (pSL3768), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsAB (pMS329), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB (pMS331) and His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB(575–613) (pGF189), the procedure described for His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was followed, except that 0.4 mM IPTG was used to induce protein expression instead of 0.3 mM. For the purification of untagged TnsAB, TnsB or TnsB(575–613), a cell pellet (corresponding to four 750 ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 30% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 1 h) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 50 ml of lysis buffer, and the proteins were eluted in a stepwise gradient (5%, 20% and 100%) of elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol). Fractions corresponding to the 20% and 100% of elution-buffer concentrations were pooled and dialysed overnight in 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HiTrap Heparin HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in dialysis buffer, washed with 30 ml of dialysis buffer and eluted in a linear gradient of heparin buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) over 150 ml (target concentration of heparin buffer: 100%). Peak fractions were pooled and further purified by SEC using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 15 mg ml−1 using a 50-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use. For the expression and purification of His6–MBP-tagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), the procedures described for untagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), respectively, were followed, except that the TEV-cleavage and heparin steps were omitted.

In a recent development, A double-stranded target DNA (dsTarget) was prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628 and oMS629 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1 ratio at a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The pull-down procedure involved mixing the assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 50 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT), 300 pmol of DNA substrate, water and 300 pmol of Cascade–TniQ and incubating this mixture at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, ATP or ATPγS (at 1 mM final concentration) was added to the sample, followed by 2,400 pmol of TnsC. The mixture was further incubated at room temperature for 30 min, after which 300 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsB(575–613) or full-length His6–MBP–TnsB was added to the sample to a final volume of 53 μl. After 30 min at room temperature, 147 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP or ATPγS) was added to the sample. Then, 10 μl were withdrawn and mixed with 10 μl of water and 5 μl of SDS dye (225 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 50% (v/v) glycerol, 5% (w/v) SDS, 0.05% (w/v) bromophenol blue, 250 mM DTT) to obtain a 5% input control sample for SDS–PAGE analysis. The sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After a short centrifugation (500g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Subsequently, 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added to the sample. After centrifugation (14,000g at 4 °C for 2 min), 20 μl of supernatant was mixed with 5 μl of SDS dye to obtain an elution sample for SDS-PAGE analysis. Next, 10 μl of 5% input control and 10 μl of elution sample were loaded on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel (Bio-Rad) for each tested condition. For the control samples Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-minus or MBP–TnsB/AB-minus, the respective SEC buffers were used instead of a protein solution. SDS-PAGE gels were imaged using a ChemiDoc Imaging system (Image Lab Touch software v.4.1, Bio-Rad) and analysed using Image Lab (v.6.1.0, Bio-Rad).

A PseCAST pDonor plasmid was first transformed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells (NEB). Single colonies were inoculated in a liquid culture and the resulting strains were made chemically competent using standard methods. PseCAST pEffector plasmids encoding a crRNA targeting the lacZ locus (crRNA-4) and all CAST subunits were transformed in the resulting strain and plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 100 µg ml−1 spectinomycin. After approximately 20 h of growth, surviving colonies were scraped from the plates, resuspended in fresh LB medium and re-plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates supplemented with 0.1 mM IPTG to induce PseCAST protein expression. Cells were incubated for an additional 18–20 h, scraped and resuspended in LB medium. Cells were then lysed and integration efficiencies were measured using qPCR as described previously1. Data were plotted and statistical analyses performed in GraphPad Prism (v.11.0.0, GraphPad). Wild-type plasmid sequences, crRNA-4 and oligonucleotides used for qPCR are listed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

The cryo-EM reconstruction of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex resulted from an initial attempt to reconstitute the QCascade–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex. Target- and donor-DNA constructs were prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS572, oMS573 and oMS576 (target; Supplementary Table 3) and oMS569, oMS570 and oMS571 (donor; Supplementary Table 3) at a 1:1:1 molar ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program involved incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. For the target pot assembly, 10× buffer (200 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1,500 mM KCl, 100 mM MgCl2, 10 mM DTT), water and TniQ–Cascade were gently mixed on ice. The target DNA was added and the sample was incubated at room temperature for 10 min. TnsC and ATP were added to the sample, which was then incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The final target pot volume was 25 μl, containing 4.5 μM of Cascade–TniQ, 4.5 μM of target DNA, 40.5 μM of TnsC, 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM DTT. The donor pot was prepared by mixing 10× buffer, water, ATP, TnsAB and donor DNA to a final volume of 25 μl (containing 18 μM TnsAB, 4.5 μM of donor DNA, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP and 1 mM DTT) and then incubating the mixture at room temperature for 10 min. However, a white insoluble precipitation was observed in the donor pot at this stage and again after mixing with the target pot and incubating at room temperature for 20 min. This was likely due to TnsAB instability under the conditions used. In fact, the donor pot components were not detected in the subsequent cryo-EM analysis. After mixing the target and donor pots, the sample was centrifuged (14,000g at 4 °C for 10 min) and the pellet discarded. Next, 2.5 μl of supernatant was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (30 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2 s (100% humidity, 4 °C) and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI), followed by storage in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system (University of Zurich, Switzerland) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 9,403 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 47 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 59.672 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

It has been revealed that in total, 9,403 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC56 live (v.4.3) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF (contrast transfer function) correction, 745,080 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300 Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 two-dimensional (2D) classes. Next, 416,193 particles were selected and three volumes were generated using ab initio reconstruction. One class yielded a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (108,814 particles) and was used for three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA; filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple); the other two volumes did not contain density for TnsC. Two distinct volumes, resulting from one 3DVA mode, were used as input for heterogeneous refinement to separate the particles of Cascade–TniQ–TnsC from those of Cascade–TniQ only. The two volumes, after a round of non-uniform refinement, were used as inputs for a second heterogeneous refinement, together with one of the volumes from the ab initio multi-class round. This refinement resulted in a volume of Cascade (195,798 particles), Cascade–TniQ (143,494 particles) and Cascade–TniQ–TnsC (76,901 particles). The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume was used for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction (76,400 particles), yielding a reconstruction at a resolution of 3.07 Å, as calculated by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (GSFSC). After particle subtraction, a local refinement of the TnsC heptamer generated a 3.44-Å (GSFSC resolution) map. A composite map was obtained by combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix57 (v.2.0-5936). Particles corresponding to Cascade only were used as an input for a 3DVA and heterogeneous refinement as described above. One of the resulting volumes, corresponding to 132,574 particles, yielded a 2.86-Å (GSFSC resolution) Cascade reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. The Cascade–TniQ volume was fed twice into a heterogeneous refinement. One of the volumes, corresponding to 50,074 particles, yielded a 3.19 Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. All maps and models have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB) (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 1). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. Monomeric initial models of Cas6, Cas7, Cas8, TniQ and TnsC were generated using AlphaFold3 (ref. 58). The AlphaFold3 models were docked manually as rigid bodies in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX59 (v.1.9). The model was real-space refined in Phenix (v.2.0-5936) against the cryo-EM map and then manually in Coot60 (v.0.9.4) using secondary structure, side chain rotamer, Ramachandran and LibG61 nucleic-acid restraints. The nucleic acid model, comprising the crRNA (positions −7 to 52), TGS (positions −60 to 4) and NTGS (positions −4 to 4, 21 to 23 and 34 to 60), was built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using PDB accession 7U5D (ref. 21) as a starting point. The cryo-EM density was clear enough to distinguish the DNA register. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 1. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1, Adobe). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1a–f.

Industry observers note that the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook recruitment complex was obtained using a pull-down approach. The dsTarget and a double-stranded right-end donor DNA (dsRE) were prepared by annealing synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628-629 and oMS576-630 (Supplementary Table 3), respectively, in a 1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The target pot was prepared by adding 1,200 pmol of dsTarget to 100 μl of assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT), after which KCl solution was added to a final KCl concentration of 230 mM and 1,200 pmol of Cascade–TniQ. The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 10 min, after which ATP and 8,400 pmol of TnsC were added. The sample was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The final target pot volume was 200 μl and its buffer composition was 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 230 mM KCl. A donor pot was prepared by mixing 1,200 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB and 1,200 pmol of dsRE substrate. The donor pot was brought to a 20 μl final volume using TnsAB SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT), mixed with the target pot and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After adding 30 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 40 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Next, 15 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added and the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 5 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. A second elution was performed using 20 μl of maltose-supplemented binding buffer, followed by three centrifugation steps as described above. The two eluates were combined into one sample and used to freeze cryo-EM grids. Two and a half microlitres of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2.5 s at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on a FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 11,374 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.947 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

In total, 11,374 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, 329,059 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300-Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 2D classes. The selected 114,608 particles were used as a training set for Topaz picking (350-Å expected particle diameter, 50 particles per micrograph), yielding 463,242 particles, which were extracted (extraction box size: 500 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 250 pixels) and classified in 150 2D classes. Classes corresponding to 189,451 particles were selected and fed into a two-class ab initio reconstruction, resulting in a junk class and a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (142,343 particles), which was used as input for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction. A 2.84-Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction was obtained from a final number of 138,834 particles, which was further used for a TnsC-focused local refinement, yielding a 2.96-Å (GSFSC resolution) volume of the heptamer decorated with additional density for each of its seven subunits. A composite map was obtained combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix (v.2.0-5936). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 2). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC model was rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The DNA duplex was extended by three nucleotides at the 5′ end of the TGS and by two nucleotides at its 3′ end, with the NTGS extended correspondingly. An initial model of the TnsC heptamer bound to seven TnsB(575–613) copies was generated using AlphaFold3 and docked manually. The model placed the last nine TnsB C-terminal residues at the additional densities of each TnsC subunit. The recognizable density of the bulky TnsB residues Trp605 and Phe612 aided in fitting the TnsB hook in the density. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 2. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1g–m.

According to recent reports, the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex was prepared using a pull-down approach. The strand-transfer substrate was prepared by annealing oligos oMS733, oMS734 and oSO146 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM each. The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. Next, 1,000 pmol of substrate, 22.5 μl of assembly buffer A (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 200 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and water were mixed with 2,000 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB to a final volume of 45 μl, and the sample was kept on ice for 10 min. In the meantime, 35.8 μl (1,000 pmol) of Cascade–TniQ was mixed with 55 μl of assembly buffer B (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and 1.6 μl of water to reduce its KCl concentration to 260 mM. This mixture was added to the initial pot and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. ATP (1 mM final concentration) was added, followed by 7,000 pmol of TnsC, reaching a final volume of 155 μl. The mixture was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After the addition of 45 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1.5 h, and after centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. After adding 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose, the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 10 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. Next, 2.5 μl of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 3 s (grid 1) or 2.5 s (grid 2) at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 43,220 movies were acquired as two separate datasets (dataset 1, 11,964 movies of grid 1; dataset 2, 31,256 movies of grid 2) at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.059 e− Å−2 (dataset 1) or 65.580 e− Å−2 (dataset 2). EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

It has been revealed that for both datasets, the exposures were imported to cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. Datasets 1 and 2 were pre-processed separately. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, particles were identified using blob picker (270–290-Å diameter, elliptical blob), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 100 2D classes. Next, 93,462 particles of dataset 1 and 203,735 of dataset 2 were selected for a two-class ab initio reconstruction, which resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume and a TnsAB tetramer volume. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC particles were re-extracted with a bigger box size (extraction box size 1,024 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 256 pixels) and used for non-uniform refinement. Using a bigger box revealed additional density at the edge of the particles, corresponding to a flexible TnsAB tetramer next to the TnsC density. This volume was low-pass filtered and used to create masks for particle subtraction. After reducing the box size (extraction box size 700 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 350 pixels), the signal for Cascade–TniQ was subtracted from the selected set of particles and the TnsABC moiety was locally refined after aligning the volume to the centre of mass of the TnsABC mask. A 3DVA (filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple) yielded one reconstruction with clear density for both TnsC and TnsAB and another with a well-resolved TnsC density but only a weak TnsAB density. The volumes were used as input for two rounds of heterogeneous refinement with the initial set of particles. Next, 49,752 were assigned to the TnsAB-bound TnsC volume, re-extracted (576 pixels) and locally refined, focusing on TnsAB. To adjust the box size for the creation of a composite map, the particles were re-extracted with a larger box-size (700 pixels) and re-aligned to the centre of mass of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC mask, yielding a 49,606-particle set. An ab initio reconstruction, followed by non-uniform refinement, resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB consensus volume at 3.10 Å GSFSC resolution. Using the consensus map, new masks were generated for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC, TnsC and TnsAB moieties as described above. The masks were used for particle subtraction of the TnsAB signal and local refinement of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex. To improve the signal of the TnsB hooks bound to TnsC, a final particle subtraction of the Cascade–TniQ signal was followed by local refinement of TnsC. The TnsAB local refinement was repeated using the final set of 49,606 particles to match the rest of the volumes. This procedure yielded focused cryo-EM maps for the TnsAB tetramer, the hook-bound TnsC heptamer and the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-hook complex at GSFSC resolutions of 3.36 Å, 3.30 Å and 3.09 Å, respectively. After re-alignment of the TnsAB volume, the global consensus map and the locally refined maps were combined into a composite map using the volume maximum function of ChimeraX (v.1.9). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 3). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 8. The QCascade–TnsC–TnsB hook model was rigid-body fitted in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The density corresponding to the tetrameric TnsAB was rigid-body fitted using our previously determined TnsAB PEC structure (PDB 9T7L)45. Missing regions in the protein and nucleic acid chains were built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) with the aid of an AlphaFold3 model of TnsAB. It was not possible to determine whether the hooks bound to TnsC could be assigned to any of the TnsB copies observed in the structure, as the region between the hook and the last modelled TnsB residue (TnsB(586-604)) is disordered. It should also be noted that the 7:7 TnsC:hook observed stoichiometry probably reflects the excess of bait (His6–MBP–TnsAB) used in pull-down preparations, rather than the physiological interaction ratio, which was observed to be 7:4 in other transpososome structures6,36,41. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 3. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the holocomplex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1n–r.

Coordinates for atomic models have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession codes 30GT (PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex), 30GB (PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex bound to TnsB hook motifs) and 30GA (PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex). 💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Lewis Nolan | 25 Nov 2026 23:55.
  • Liverpool are seriously considering re-signing Jarell Quansah from Bayer Leverkusen in 2027, the latest report has claimed.
  • Andoni Iraola's side emerged as 3-0 winners against Club Brugge in the Champions League on Wednesday, with the Merseysiders keeping a second consecutive clean sheet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lewis Nolan | 25 Nov 2026 23:55.

Liverpool are seriously considering re-signing Jarell Quansah from Bayer Leverkusen in 2027, the latest report has claimed.

Andoni Iraola's side emerged as 3-0 winners against Club Brugge in the Champions League on Wednesday, with the Merseysiders keeping a second consecutive clean sheet.

Captain Virgil van Dijk started on the bench, before coming on to add more solidity at the back alongside Jeremy Jacquet.

Van Dijk has been exceptional once again this season, but with his contract set to expire at the end of the current campaign, Iraola could soon be in the market for a replacement.

TEAMtalk have claimed that former Red Quansah has emerged as a serious target, though Liverpool's buy-back clause of £50m will expire after the coming summer transfer window, meaning a decision about signing him will have to be made in the coming months.

Quansah is a strong passer of the ball ane has demonstrated in the past that he is capable of coming out on top in battles in the air, though he has struggled to settle this season.

In the 2026-27 Bundesliga, the centre-back has only completed 42.3 passes per match and has won just 32% of his aerial duels, something that may be a major concern to Liverpool given he is 6ft 3in.

The 23-year-old completed 52.8 passes per game last season in the league, while he also won 60% of his aerial duels.

There are concerns about Quansah's recovery defending and temperament inside the box, so perhaps Liverpool should look elsewhere in the summer for the heir to Van Dijk.

The unfortunate reality for Liverpool is that they will have to become accustomed to life without Van Dijk sooner rather than later.

However, there is nothing to suggest based on his current form that the 35-year-old cannot continue to play at the highest level for at least another season.

As long as Van Dijk can continue to dominate attackers and use his immense recovery pace, then Liverpool should look to extend their captain's contract.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.
  • Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.
  • On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

It has been revealed that guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

What a strike from Nicolas Jackson to beat Gianluigi Donnarumma 😲 Villa Park erupts 🔊 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/zkuDVMevKF.

Maresca said: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”.

When asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca said: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”.

While much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

Industry observers note that it was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery mentioned: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

In a recent development, “Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”.

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

Industry observers note that with City appearing to take control, Emery responded by introducing fresh £47m signing Ibrahim Mbaye from the bench and it proved an inspired decision. Mbaye was sent clear on the right by Jackson and then provided the assist for his international team-mate, with the forward’s shot embarrassing Donnarumma by going underneath his left hand.

Recent findings suggest that for a long time, football has a system where you can tell who deserved to win or not. It is the scoreboard. For decades, longer even, you could tell who was the better team by looking at who had the most goals.

However, football managers persist with the idea that there is another ineffable reason that decides who deserves what. Enzo Maresca is apparently no different.

He told the BBC: “When we scored I had the feeling that we were in control and really for the entire game. We created many chances but unfortunately didn’t score them. We conceded one transition in the second half and they were very efficient because they scored. Bit unlucky and we learn from that.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

It has been revealed that however, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

In a recent development, emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • FC Barcelona’s third defeat this season, in all competitions, will not have happened this Wednesday.
  • It has been revealed that with Lamine Yamal diminished and absent from the match sheet, Hansi Flick lined up a somewhat reshuffled eleven.
  • But this episode past, it was the Catalans who gradually got their foot on the ball.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FC Barcelona’s third defeat this season, in all competitions, will not have happened this Wednesday. And it’s no surprise since the Catalans were away to the very modest Sabah FC. Against the Azerbaijani club, Barça logically won their match on the 5th day of the Champions League league phase (1-4).

It has been revealed that with Lamine Yamal diminished and absent from the match sheet, Hansi Flick lined up a somewhat reshuffled eleven. Gabriel Jesus, for example, started up front, while Jules Koundé started in the right lane. The locals courageously tried their luck at the start of the match and even found the crossbar on a strike from Ivan Lepinjica (27th).

But this episode past, it was the Catalans who gradually got their foot on the ball. Anthony Gordon ended up opening the scoring after half an hour of play (0-1, 31st). Two minutes later, the Englishman thought he had his double, but the VAR signaled an offside (33rd).

Regardless, the former Newcastle player was back at the start of the second half and made the break for Barça (0-2, 51st). Too complicated for Sabah FC who failed a third time with a goal from Karim Adeyemi (0-3, 55th). And a fourth when Gabriel Jesus found the fault in his turn (0-4, 60th).

From then on, the visitors took their foot off the gas. A boon for the locals who reduced the gap and saved the honor by Joy Mickels (1-4, 63rd). The end of the meeting will be soporific. Note, however, a newly introduced injury on the Barça side with the premature exit of Alejandro Balde (64th). This success allows the Blaugrana to temporarily move up to fourth place in the standings. Sabah is thirty-second.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Before this, Ruben Amorim’s squad was already looking short – an issue which most have felt was the case since before the summer – and now it’s gotten shorter again, somehow.

GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller manufacturer she worked for.

In a recent development, alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing organization. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed notes it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

Sources indicate that at the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it noted. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.".

According to recent reports, the US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the Newly introduced York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

According to recent reports, megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the firm's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The newspaper noted that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country .
  • Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception.
  • In a recent development, but when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

In a recent development, but when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can.".

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

It has been revealed that although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

Industry observers note that the match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

Recent findings suggest that at some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment.".

According to recent reports, for now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

Published: 18:46 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:51 EST, 24 November 2026.

Hibernian ended their long wait for a Premiership home win after overcoming Dundee in a hard-fought contest at Easter Road.

Martin Boyle and Nicky Cadden – who curled home a stunning effort from outside the box – had the hosts in command before the interval.

But Dundee, still licking their wounds after an 8-0 savaging at the hands of Hearts on Saturday, indicated plenty of fight after the break and pulled one back through Joe Wright.

The visitors tried in vain to grab an equaliser and it was Hibs who were left satisfied by their first three points at home since beating Kilmarnock on April 4.

Manager Marink Reedijk was thrilled to have bounced back from their 4-0 weekend home defeat at the hands of Dundee United, saying: ‘I think it’s a good reaction to what we have done against Dundee United.

Industry observers note that ‘It’s important that you get the three points at home. Again, that’s a massive win. I saw a front foot team again, I saw togetherness again, I saw a team who fought for every ball.

Martin Boyle takes the acclaim after scoring the all-key second goal for Hibernian.

‘That’s not easy, they have to be patient, you have to be secure, you have to wait for your moment and we took these moments and that was really good to see.

Recent findings suggest that ‘The goal of Nicky [Cadden] is one to, we say, put in a frame and put on your wall as a painting. The one of Martin [Boyle] is why Martin is so important for us. He can disrupt an opponent if they are so organised and so close to each other and so deep.

‘As long as we keep ourselves, I think these are good signs.’.

It has been revealed that hibs played on the front foot as they looked to start repairing the damage from the weekend. On a rare start, Togo international Thibault Klidje was lively and saw a header crash into the side-netting before hitting a harmless snap-shot straight at Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman.

From a short corner routine Hibs worked space for Cadden on the edge of the box from Josh Mulligan’s lay-off and his driving effort whistled just past a post.

It has been revealed that dundee were desperate to keep it tight at the back but offered little going forward. Just when it looked like they were beginning to settle Hibs hit them with two goals in three minutes before the break.

The first came in the 40th minute when Boyle fired a penalty past Goodman after being tripped by Ryan Finnigan.

Nicky Cadden unleashes an absolute pearler into the top corner to put Hibs in front.

Cadden then found the top corner with a sublime curling effort from his left foot just outside the box. It was another short corner routine that saw Miguel Chaiwa set up the wing-back.

Despite the hammer blow of losing two goals in quick succession before the break, Dundee demonstrated at the start of the second half that they were not going to roll over.

Steven Pressley’s side upped their intensity as they searched for a goal to get themselves back in the game and that arrived in the 67th minute courtesy of Wright.

Substitute Callum Jones’ free-kick should have been put away by Ryan Astley but the ball broke back to Wright and he slammed the ball high into the net from six yards.

That set up a tense finish but Hibs desperately held on for a rare home victory.

For Pressley, who changed half of his outfield XI following his side’s weekend humiliation, there were also positives to take.

According to recent reports, the Dark Blues boss mentioned: ‘We’re disappointed to not come away with anything and to obviously lose the game. But I also thought we restored some degree of pride tonight.

‘Going into half-time 2-0 down, losing two late goals in the half, can be a little bit demoralising, especially for a team that has a bit of fragility on the back of the weekend’s result.

Sources indicate that ‘I thought we responded brilliantly. We demonstrated a lot of courage, a lot of determination, a lot of spirit and, as I’ve remarked, I think we certainly restored some level of pride that allows us a foundation to move into the weekend.’.

By Joel Lefevre | 26 Nov 2026 01:21, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 01:22.

Needing a victory to keep their MLS season alive, the Portland Timbers will host Dallas in game two of that best-of-three series on Saturday at Providence Park.

The opener went to Los Toros in Frisco, 3-0, putting them one win away from the Western Conference semi-finals for the first time since 2022.

For the second successive campaign, the Timbers face a must-win situation heading into game two of the playoffs after lacking decisiveness in the attacking third last Saturday.

Portland have not made it beyond the opening round of the playoffs since their run to the MLS Cup final in 2021, losing to New York City FC on penalties that year.

They are now 12-10-8 all-time in post-season outings, while winning just one of their last seven playoff games in normal time.

That said, Marti Cifuentes has seen his side lose just one of their last six league fixtures at Providence Park, winning those last two matches and scoring three goals both times.

In addition to that, this club have gone on to win their last two post-season matches at home, while suffering just one playoff defeat this decade at Providence Park in 90 minutes.

The Timbers have never lost a playoff home game versus Dallas in normal time, though their last post-season win against them at Providence Park occurred in 2015 (3-1).

After a cagey opening 45 minutes in game one, Dallas took command in the second half last week, putting themselves in the driver’s seat to advance.

Whatever Eric Quill is saying to this group at half-time, the message has been well received, with his team outscoring opponents by a combined 6-1 margin in the second half of their last two games.

A triumph on Saturday would snap a three-match MLS winless run for the Texas club away from home and mark their first playoff victory as the visitors since beating the Timbers on penalties in Portland in 2020.

Since that triumph, Dallas have failed to score in four of their last five post-season affairs which took place outside of Frisco.

In 2026, they have conceded in all but three MLS road outings, while allowing three or more goals on four separate occasions.

Los Toros can extend their winning run versus Portland to three matches on Saturday, while they are unbeaten in eight successive meetings against them.

Dallas Major League Soccer form:.

Do not expect to see Juan David Mosquera on the field for the Timbers Saturday as he recovers from a foot and ankle issue, while Zac McGraw has a sore back, Brandon Bye is dealing with a knee injury and Alex Bonetig is doubtful due to a shoulder strain.

Cole Bassett and Kristoffer Velde were the most dangerous Portland players in game one, each with three shots, while James Pantemis made five stops in a losing effort.

At Dallas, Anderson Julio is questionable for this match because of a lower-body injury after sitting out in the opening game of this series.

Joaquin Valiente registered his first career playoff brace in game one, with Sam Sarver scoring his first MLS post-season goal in that victory.

Portland Timbers possible starting lineup:.

Pantemis; Hernandez, K. Miller, Waterman, Fory; Bassett, Chara, Da Costa; Velde, Janssen, Lassiter.

Dallas possible starting lineup:.

Daniel; Johansson, Urhoghide, Moore, Norris; Valiente, Kaick, Ramiro, Binyamin; Musa, Sarver.

#117560. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
