#117491. Breaking: What's going on with the polar vortex?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (676 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What's going on with the polar vortex?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that high up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons.
  • If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that high up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event.".

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It has been revealed that it's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

Industry observers note that but bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

Recent findings suggest that for example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

According to recent reports, some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

In a recent development, A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

Industry observers note that “I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”.

And how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

With the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP.

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

“I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two big chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”.

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an important moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite rapidly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

According to recent reports, everything with Isak feels to be going under the radar at the moment, but that is six goals in six Premier League appearances. He is starting to show the consistency and killer instinct that everyone felt he would. Iraola will be hoping it continues for the foreseeable future.

“The performance was really good,” stated Isak, the quiet assassin. “We were really solid against a really good team. The first half is what we really want to be about. It was about intensity, winning balls and countering.”.

It has been revealed that brighton, as much as Hürzeler protested, could not properly recover, though this is no criticism. They remain committed to attack, they struck the frame of the goal when Ayari tried to punish an Alisson Becker mistake and the desire to keep pushing ensured Liverpool could never relax.

What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

Industry observers note that they remember those moments as much as the stardust that Barcola and Isak provide. Put it all together and it might just be a launchpad for Iraola.

Ngumoha has always had feet that move as promptly as the hands of street artists who perform tricks with cups and balls: now you see it, now you don’t. We live in an age where talent is quickly amplified and this young England international has it in bundles.

You saw it in those exhilarating 74 minutes: Ngumoha had his most touches in a game this campaign (51), most touches in the opposition box (12) and attempted the most dribbles (10), as well as creating the most chances (three) and providing two assists.

It is the first time an 18-year-old has produced such figures in the Champions League since Opta’s European records began in 2008-09.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Liverpool and Brighton & Hove Albion at Anfield.

Industry observers note that liverpool are on a three-game winning run in all competitions, and came from two goals behind in their previous outing in the Champions League on Tuesday, earning an enthralling 4-3 victory over Villarreal. Last weekend, Andoni Iraola’s men also initially fell behind against Brentford in the Premier League, but netted two second-half goals through Daniel Munoz and Alexander Isak to win 2-1 as their opponents finished with nine men.

In his programme notes, Liverpool boss Iraola was excited about the prospect of a second game in a week at home. “As someone who believes every single opportunity we have to play a game at this stadium and in front of our supporters is a privilege, I also feel very passionately that this is a period that we should continue to embrace,” he noted.

Sources indicate that “It is also a spell in which we will carry on being tested because the quality of the opposition dictates that there is no chance of anything else. Villarreal pushed us all the way in midweek and everything about the way Brighton have played so far this season tells us that it would be foolish to expect anything but the same today.”.

According to recent reports, brighton have emerged as one of the surprise packages of the Premier League season thanks to their blistering start. Fabian Hurzeler’s side sit third in the table, having scored a whopping 23 goals in their opening seven games, while conceding just five. On Thursday, Brighton were unexpectedly held to a 0-0 draw by Czech outfit Jablonec, ending a run of six straight victories in all competitions. Nevertheless, they’re unbeaten since their 4-3 league loss to Chelsea back on August 30.

Industry observers note that defender Ferdi Kadioglu believes his team’s energy and fitness has played a huge role in their eye-catching form. “If you want to play how we play, you have to be very fit,” he mentioned. “We were already fit last season, but I think it’s more that now everyone really understands what we need to do to win matches. That’s really clear this season, and everyone is doing it. Everyone is really focused on their task and doing it very well so far.”.

Rasmus Hojlund has laid bare the suffocating pressure of playing for Manchester United and given his insight into what Mauricio Pochettino’s squad will be suffering while marooned in the Premier League relegation zone.

The Dane was back in town this week after spending two seasons at United, mocking Manchester City fans when scoring the opener of Napoli’s 2-2 draw at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday night.

Hojlund secured a £38million permanent move away from Old Trafford in the summer but remains in touch with plenty of old team-mates and believes the lack of equilibrium at the club has contributed to a steady decline.

‘There are so many people following the club around the world and you can’t really escape from it,’ Hojlund said.

Recent findings suggest that ‘It is almost too high when it is good and almost too low when it is bad. It is all about trying to be in that middle. I had both the highs and the lows there.

It has been revealed that ‘The pressure is part of the club, it comes with playing for United. There has been a lot of change but hopefully they will get it right with Mauricio.’.

Rasmus Hojlund mocked Man City fans after scoring for Napoli at the Etihad on Tuesday night.

Industry observers note that A United supporter, Hojlund laughed off the idea that the club is in a relegation scrap despite their worst start to a season since 1972. And the 23-year-old revealed that the players were ready for ‘change’ following the sacking of Michael Carrick.

‘I spoke with Bruno [Fernandes] and Diogo [Dalot] during the international break and they were all obviously devastated that Michael was going but also looking forward to some change,’ Hojlund added.

‘I am still speaking with Patrick [Dorgu] and I just wish the guys all the best. I am sure they will turn it around this season. They have got a lot of quality. They have got a great squad, good leaders, good professionals.

‘It is a temporary picture, I think they will get back to the top. The Premier League is like this. I read the other day that Bournemouth was in the relegation zone after a couple of games, now they have won the last five games and are in the top half of the table.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer claims she was accused of political and military espionage.

Recent findings suggest that but, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

In a recent development, opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Sources indicate that verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Sources indicate that such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan noted that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Recent findings suggest that espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, mentioned the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

Sources indicate that on the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law.".

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas mentioned.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security matter.".

It has been revealed that in terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

According to recent reports, this suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

Recent findings suggest that in some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas stated that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment.".

Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 95 min read (19010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~95 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2.
  • It has been revealed that somatic and germline pathogenic variants in cancer-associated genes cause diverse congenital disorders1,2 and are also found in phenotypically normal tissue4,5.
  • It has been revealed that PIK3CA encodes p110α, the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3Kα), which regulates cell growth, proliferation, migration and metabolism6 through AKT and downstream effectors, including mTOR and forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factors7,8.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2. Among the affected tissues, the endothelium commonly exhibits aberrant expansion, leading to vascular malformations3. Notably, these lesions arise predominantly in veins and capillaries, whereas arteries are largely spared, for reasons that remain unclear. Here, using genetic lineage tracing, we show that endothelial expression of PIK3CAH1047R drives profound clonal expansion of capillary and venous endothelial cells, whereas mature arterial endothelial cells are refractory to pathological PI3K activation. Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features, providing a mechanistic explanation for the paucity of arterial lesions after PIK3CA genetic perturbation. Mechanistically, these effects are mediated by two complementary downstream branches of PI3K signalling: increased proliferation, which drives vascular overgrowth, and upregulation of the venous-specifying transcription factor NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), which suppresses arterial differentiation. Together, our findings reveal that pathogenic responses to PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial differentiation state and fate trajectory, and demonstrate that arterial endothelium is intrinsically resistant to oncogenic PI3K signalling. Arteries are therefore shielded from PIK3CA mutations, explaining the rarity of arterial malformations in PIK3CA-driven disease.

It has been revealed that somatic and germline pathogenic variants in cancer-associated genes cause diverse congenital disorders1,2 and are also found in phenotypically normal tissue4,5. Germline mutations may be inherited or arise de novo, whereas somatic mutations, acquired during embryonic development, generate mosaicism and a broad spectrum of phenotypes1. Understanding how identical mutations produce distinct outcomes across tissues is crucial for defining cellular susceptibility to disease and explaining the phenotypic heterogeneity.

It has been revealed that PIK3CA encodes p110α, the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3Kα), which regulates cell growth, proliferation, migration and metabolism6 through AKT and downstream effectors, including mTOR and forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factors7,8. PIK3CA is an oncogene that is frequently mutated in both mosaic congenital disorders9 and phenotypically normal tissue4. Activating mutations occur throughout the coding sequence, with recurrent hotspots including E545K, E542K, H1047R and H1047L3. Mesoderm-derived tissues, including the endothelium, are commonly affected in PIK3CA-related congenital disorders, which manifest as aberrant tissue overgrowth and vascular malformations10,11,12,13. Although PIK3CA mutations have been extensively studied in adult epithelial tissues14,15,16,17, their effects on cellular heterogeneity, differentiation and clonal dynamics in mesoderm-derived lineages remain poorly understood.

Industry observers note that vascular malformations are congenital vascular anomalies classified as slow-flow lesions, affecting capillaries, veins and lymphatic vessels or fast-flow lesions, often involving arteries18. Somatic activating PIK3CA mutations occur in the endothelium of all major slow-flow vascular malformations, where lesion expansion requires mitogenic signals, even though the mutation alone is insufficient to confer a proliferative advantage19,20,21,22. By contrast, no evidence currently implicates PIK3CA mutations in fast-flow arterial malformations3. Whether arterial endothelial cells have these mutations but resist their effects, or mutant clones are negatively selected or eliminated in arterial vessels remains unclear.

Here we demonstrate that endothelial responses to oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R are governed by cellular identity and developmental trajectory. Combining mosaic genetics, lineage tracing and single-cell analyses, we identify a differentiation-stage-specific window of susceptibility to pathological PI3K signalling, while fully differentiated arterial endothelial cells are resistant. These findings provide a framework for the tissue and vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

Postnatal expression of Pik3caH1047R (Pik3catm1.1Waph/+) from the endogenous locus in mouse retinal endothelial cells using Pdgfb-creERT2 results in venous and capillary malformations, whereas arteries remain unaffected19 (Extended Data Fig. 1a–e). To correlate these phenotypes with the distribution of mutant cells, we introduced the R26-mTmG reporter allele into the Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice (pan-endothelial (pEC)-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 1a). Tamoxifen-mediated Cre activation induced recombination of the endogenous Pik3caH1047R allele and the reporter, resulting in membrane-bound GFP expression that marks recombined cells and therefore approximates Pik3caH1047R-expressing endothelial cells. Pdgfb-creERT2R26-mTmG mice were used as controls (pEC-GFP). After low-dose administration of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at postnatal day 1 (P1), retinas were analysed at P6 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Mosaic recombination was observed throughout the vascular plexus in both genotypes (Fig. 1b). Although GFP+ mutant cells were present in all vessel types, vascular malformations occurred exclusively in capillaries and veins (Fig. 1c,d). In these vessels, mutant GFP+ endothelial cells underwent marked clonal expansion, generating enlarged vascular tubes (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1f), accompanied by increased endothelial cell proliferation during early lesion formation (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i). By contrast, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells in arteries neither expanded nor altered vessel width (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Consistent with these phenotypes, capillary and venous mutant GFP+ cells displayed increased PI3K pathway activation, as assessed by staining of phosphorylated S6 (p-S6), whereas arterial mutant cells showed no detectable increase relative to wild-type (WT) cells (Fig. 1d,f). These data show that Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells selectively expand in capillaries and veins, while arteries remain structurally and molecularly normal despite containing mutant cells.

a, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and endothelial populations targeted by low-dose 4-OHT-induced Pdgfb-creERT2 activation; pEC, pan-endothelial cells. b, Confocal images of P6 retinas stained for IB4 (red, blood vessels) and GFP (cyan/grey, Pdgfb-targeted endothelial cells). c, The incidence of vascular malformations in P6 pEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas (n = 8 retinas). d, High-magnification confocal images of P6 retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (Ser235/236) (yellow/grey, PI3K readout). The white dotted rectangles indicate the regions magnified on the right. e,f, Quantification of GFP+ area (n = 13, 19, 5, 15, 5 and 13 retinas, left to right) (e) and p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ areas (n = 6, 8, 5, 8, 5 and 7 retinas, left to right) (f) in capillaries, veins and arteries. g, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and endothelial population targeted by 4-OHT-induced Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 activation. aEC, arterial endothelial cells. h,i, Confocal images of P9 aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan, Bmx-targeted endothelial cells) (h) or IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (grey) (i). j,k, GFP+ arterial area (n = 6 and 11 retinas, left to right) (j) and p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ areas (n = 6 and 7 retinas, left to right) (k). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (e,f,j,k). Scale bars, 150 μm (b,h) and 30 μm (d,i). FC, fold change; NS, not significant.

Industry observers note that the apparent resistance of arterial endothelial cells to Pik3caH1047R prompted us to directly investigate the behaviour of mutant cells in arteries. To this end, we used the Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 mouse line, which specifically targets arterial endothelial cells in retinal vessels. WT and Pik3caH1047R arterial endothelial cells (aEC) were traced by combining Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 and R26-mTmG with or without the Pik3caH1047R allele (aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 1g). Bmx(PAC)-creERT2-mediated tracing revealed robust arterial recombination after 4-OHT administration at P4 or P7, whereas induction at P1 did not label arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). Thus, recombination was induced at P4 or P7 for subsequent experiments. In both settings, the proportion of GFP+ cells and arterial vessel width were comparable between the mutant and control retinas (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 2c–f). Arteries also displayed similar smooth-muscle-cell coverage and maintained expression of arterial markers UNC5B and CX37 (Extended Data Fig. 2g–j). Moreover, GFP+ arterial endothelial cells of both genotypes lacked expression of NR2F2, a key transcription factor that suppresses arterial identity23,24,25,26 (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). Consistent with earlier observations, mutant GFP+ cells showed low PI3K pathway activation, with no increase relative to controls (Fig. 1i,k and Extended Data Fig. 2m,n). To assess the long-term effects, we analysed retinas at P21. No differences were detected in the GFP+ cell distribution, arterial morphology or NR2F2 expression between WT and Pik3caH1047R cells in main arteries and arteriolar branches (Extended Data Fig. 2o–q). These findings show that mutant cells persist in arteries or arteriolar branches without detectable changes in arterial identity, morphology or PI3K activation, supporting the resistance of differentiated arterial endothelial cells to Pik3caH1047R.

To investigate why arterial endothelial cells are protected against Pik3caH1047R, we pharmacologically disrupted key arterial features in aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R pups. As arterial endothelial cells experience higher shear stress, we first reduced systemic blood pressure with the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor captopril27. Although captopril reduced KLF4 expression and induced dilation of the vascular plexus28, it did not alter the proportion of GFP+ cells or arterial width. Furthermore, endothelial proliferation was not increased in mutant arteries (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d). We next inhibited Notch signalling, a key regulator of arterial differentiation and maintenance, using N-[N-(3,5-difluorophenacetyl)-l-alanyl]-S-phenylglycine t-butyl ester (DAPT). Despite a pronounced response in sprouting capillaries, DAPT likewise did not elicit any response in arteries to Pik3caH1047R expression (Extended Data Fig. 3a,e,f). Collectively, these results indicate that inhibition of major arterial identity programmes alone is insufficient to overcome arterial resistance to Pik3caH1047R.

To test whether resistance to Pik3caH1047R emerges during arterial differentiation, we traced tip endothelial cells—a pre-arterial population that contributes to arterial growth29,30. We used the Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mouse line, which specifically marks tip cells, crossed with R26-mTmG (tEC-GFP) alone or in combination with Pik3caH1047R (tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 2a). 4-OHT was administered at P1, and Esm1-GFP+ progeny were analysed at different timepoints (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Then, 24 h after induction, GFP+ cells were predominantly localized at the sprouting front (Fig. 2b). By P6, GFP+ cells contributed extensively to arteries in tEC-GFP retinas, and the GFP+ arterial area further increased by P8 (Fig. 2b). Consistent with previous reports30, a subset of Esm1-traced cells also contributed to the capillary plexus (Fig. 2b). Pik3caH1047R expression markedly reduced the GFP+ area within arteries (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Instead, most mutant GFP+ cells were retained in the capillary bed, where they expanded (Fig. 2d,f and Extended Data Fig. 4b–f) and formed multiple vascular malformations (Fig. 2b,c). Moreover, mutant, but not control, GFP+ cells were frequently detected in veins (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). The few Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells that reached arteries did not induce pathology (Fig. 2c). Consistent with lesion formation, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells displayed increased p-S6 levels in capillaries, but not in arteries (Fig. 2e,g and Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). By P21, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ clones persisted in capillaries and veins, although they did not further expand (Extended Data Fig. 4i–l). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R expression impairs mobilization of arterial precursors to arteries, resulting in their retention within capillaries and the diversion of a subset towards veins, where they expand and form vascular malformations.

Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (f,g,l,m). Scale bars, 150 μm (b,i) and 30 μm (d,e,k).

To directly compare WT and mutant endothelial cells within the same tissue, we generated a multispectral genetic mouse model, termed iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R). Cre-mediated recombination stochastically generates either His-H2B-Cherry (WT) or H2B-eGFP-V5 together with HA-PIK3CAH1047R (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Validation in primary endothelial cells confirmed preferential generation of Cherry+ cells, as reported for related constructs31, and increased proliferation and PI3K pathway activation in eGFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5b–h). To fate-map pre-arterial endothelial cells in vivo, we crossed iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice with Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mice (tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) (Fig. 2h). As the recombination efficiency was lower than in Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, we increased the 4-OHT dose, and retinas were analysed 7 days after induction (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cherry+ cells contributed to both capillaries and arteries (Fig. 2i–k). By contrast, eGFP+ cells were predominantly located in capillaries, including those adjacent to arteries, and in veins, where they expanded and formed vascular malformations (Fig. 2i–k and Extended Data Fig. 6b). eGFP+ cells greatly outnumbered Cherry+ cells (7,680 versus 511) and displayed increased Ki-67 positivity and p-S6 levels (Fig. 2j,l,m and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Despite their expansion, only 0.47% of total eGFP+ cells was incorporated into arteries, compared with 23% of Cherry+ cells (Fig. 2j). Overall, mutant endothelial cells were detected in only 16% of arteries containing recombined cells (Fig. 2n). Co-staining for eGFP, Cherry and ERG confirmed that lesions consisted exclusively of mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 6e).

In contrast to Esm1+ cells expressing Pik3caH1047R from the endogenous locus, which did not induce arterial pathology (Fig. 2c,e), all eGFP+ cells that reached arteries in the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model formed small lesions (averaging nine cells per lesion) (Fig. 2k). We therefore tested whether forced overexpression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial endothelial cells would produce a similar phenotype. To this end, we combined iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R with Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 and induced recombination between P4 and P6, or between P7 and P9 (Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Five days later, the expected proportions of Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells were detected (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Mutant arterial cells remained non-pathogenic after late recombination; however, targeting at P4–6 resulted in mild arterial overgrowth in around 20% of arteries containing recombined mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Across models, arterial width inversely correlated with endothelial differentiation state at the time of PIK3CAH1047R expression (Extended Data Fig. 6i). eGFP+ arterial endothelial cells revealed increased PI3K signalling activation compared with neighbouring Cherry+ cells under all conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6g,j). By contrast, endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression did not increase arterial p-S6 levels (Figs. 1d,f,i,k and 2e,g). Nonetheless, eGFP+ arterial cells still lacked NR2F2 expression (Extended Data Fig. 6k), consistent with maintained arterial identity. Together, these data indicate that arterial resistance to PIK3CAH1047R depends on endothelial differentiation state and mutant expression level. Forced overexpression partially overcomes this resistance at earlier developmental stages, promoting mild arterial overgrowth without inducing NR2F2 expression.

To investigate how Pik3caH1047R impairs arterial mobilization, we analysed endothelial cell transcriptomes using single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. We profiled endothelial cells from tEC-GFP (6,564 cells) and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R (19,168 cells) retinas, enabling molecular tracing of Esm1+ tip cells and their progeny (Fig. 3a). We first defined endothelial transcriptional states in WT retinas by clustering scRNA-seq data from tEC-GFP retinas. Unsupervised analysis identified nine populations: tip, pre-arterial angiogenic, metabolic angiogenic, proliferative 1, proliferative 2, venous, capillary, arterial capillary and arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c and Supplementary Data 1). Notably, hierarchical clustering based on average gene expression profiles grouped tip, proliferative and metabolic angiogenic populations together, whereas pre-arterial angiogenic endothelial cells were more similar to arterial and arterial-capillary populations, supporting their arterial bias (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Traced cells were identified by GFP transcripts (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Projection of GFP expression onto the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) revealed Esm1-traced cells in all clusters except for the venous population (Extended Data Fig. 7f–h). Approximately half of Esm1-traced cells localized to arterial populations, whereas around 20% remained proliferative, indicating that Esm1-derived endothelial cells normally retain proliferative capacity while progressively differentiating into the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7h).

The dot size and colour indicate the frequency and expression level, respectively. d, UMAP of GFP+ endothelial cells (Esm1-derived progeny) from tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas. e, The distribution of GFP+ endothelial cells across clusters. f, Differential gene expression between GFP+ mutant and WT endothelial cells across clusters, highlighting arterial, tip/pre-arterial and venous-associated signatures. The dot colour indicates the log2-transformed FC value and the size indicates significance (adjusted P < 0.05). g, Confocal images of P6 sprouting fronts stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and UNC5B (yellow). The white and red arrows indicate ERG+NR2F2− and ERG+NR2F2+ cells within the GFP+ area, respectively. i, UNC5B fluorescence in GFP+ cells at the sprouting front (n = 4 retinas). j, The percentage of NR2F2+ERG+ nuclei relative to total ERG+ nuclei within GFP+ capillary areas (n = 6 and 5 retinas, left to right). According to recent reports, we next examined whether Pik3caH1047R affects this developmental trajectory. To address this, we jointly analysed WT and Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells. Integrated analysis resolved seven endothelial populations: tip (C1), metabolic angiogenic (C2), proliferative 1 (C3), proliferative 2 (C4), venous (C5), arterial capillary (C6) and arterial (C7) endothelial cells (Fig. 3b,c, Extended Data Fig. 7i and Supplementary Data 1). GFP expression revealed a marked redistribution of Esm1-traced cells (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7j,k). Whereas WT GFP+ cells predominantly localized to arterial capillary and arterial clusters (C6 and C7), Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells were instead enriched within angiogenic, proliferative and venous clusters (C2, C3, C4 and C5) (Fig. 3d,e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Quantification confirmed selective expansion of mutant GFP+ cells in proliferative, angiogenic and venous clusters, but not arterial clusters (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Importantly, Pik3ca expression was comparable across all endothelial clusters (Extended Data Fig. 7l).

Sources indicate that to determine whether this redistribution also reflected altered endothelial transcriptional identity, we performed cluster-specific differential expression analysis comparing GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial populations. We identified transcriptional alterations between WT and mutant cells in all clusters, with only limited changes in arterial cells (C7), consistent with the resistance observed in differentiated arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7m). The tip cluster (C1) contained too few cells for robust differential expression analysis (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Affected clusters showed a consistent shift towards venous-associated gene expression, accompanied by reduced tip, arterial, guidance and capillary-specialization programmes (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 7n). This pattern remained after correcting for differences in cluster size (Supplementary Fig. 1). Hierarchical clustering further showed the greatest genotype-dependent divergence in angiogenic and venous populations (Extended Data Fig. 7o). We next performed RNA velocity analysis on subclustered GFP+ cells, which revealed altered cell-state dynamics in Esm1-traced mutant endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7p,q and Supplementary Data 1). Whereas WT GFP+ cells displayed coherent trajectories toward capillary and arterial states, mutant cells showed altered cell-state trajectories, with prominent progression toward proliferative and venous-associated populations and reduced progression toward the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7r). Together, these findings indicate that Pik3caH1047R promotes endothelial proliferation while diverting differentiating endothelial cells away from the arterial programme towards venous-associated cell states.

To determine whether this programme is initiated rapidly after Pik3caH1047R expression, we analysed cultured sister endothelial cells derived from Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice using scRNA-seq (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b and Supplementary Data 2). Endothelial identity across clusters was confirmed by uniform Pecam1 expression, and Pik3ca expression was comparable between clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). Acute Pik3caH1047R expression recapitulated the in vivo transcriptional changes, with expansion of proliferative and venous-like populations and reduction of tip/arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 8e–g). Mutant cells also expressed higher levels of venous markers (that is, Nr2f2 and Nrp2) and lower levels of tip markers (that is, Esm1 and Angpt2) (Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R rapidly and cell-autonomously initiates a programme of proliferation and loss of arterial identity.

Industry observers note that we next examined how this transcriptional transition unfolds during arterial differentiation in vivo by staining tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas at P4 and P6 for UNC5B and NR2F2. Control GFP+ cells expressed UNC5B by P4 while remaining NR2F2 negative at both timepoints (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–l). Mutant GFP+ cells were similar to controls at P4 but, by P6, revealed reduced UNC5B expression at the sprouting front and near arteries, along with ectopic NR2F2 expression (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–n). These findings validate the scRNA-seq data and demonstrate that Pik3caH1047R progressively disrupts arterial differentiation in vivo.

To establish the temporal relationship between hyperproliferation and arterial differentiation defects, we examined the proliferative behaviour of Esm1-traced cells at P4 and P6. EdU incorporation highlighted that Esm1-traced cells normally retain proliferative capacity at P4, with proliferation beginning to diminish by P6 (Fig. 3k–m). Pik3caH1047R mutant Esm1-traced cells exhibited the same temporal pattern, although proliferation remained markedly higher at both timepoints, indicating that hyperproliferation precedes ectopic NR2F2 induction (Fig. 3k–m). The absence of a further increase in proliferation after NR2F2 induction at P6 argues against NR2F2 driving endothelial hyperproliferation.

In a recent development, to test whether hyperproliferation accounts for defective arterial differentiation, we treated tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice with the CDK4 and CDK6 inhibitor palbociclib. Palbociclib partially reduced endothelial proliferation and vascular hyperplasia in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas but did not restore arterial differentiation or suppress NR2F2 expression (Fig. 4a–h). Similar results were obtained with mitomycin C, which robustly inhibited endothelial expansion without restoring arterial incorporation or reducing NR2F2 expression in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a–i). Consistently, palbociclib inhibited cell cycle progression in vitro but did not prevent Pik3caH1047R-driven NR2F2 upregulation (Fig. 4i–k and Extended Data Fig. 9j–m). Together, these findings show that suppressing proliferation does not prevent NR2F2 induction or restore arterial differentiation, supporting distinct effects of Pik3caH1047R signalling on proliferation and arterial specification. Consistent with this interpretation, scRNA-seq analysis revealed no association between Nr2f2 expression and cell cycle status in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 10a).

Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA with Šidák’s multiple-comparison test (c–g,i,j). Scale bars, 100 μm (b) and 20 μm (h).

As Pik3caH1047R induces NR2F2 expression in pre-arterial endothelial cells, and NR2F2 suppresses arterial identity23,24,25,26, we hypothesized that NR2F2 mediates the arterial differentiation defect downstream of Pik3caH1047R. To test this hypothesis, we crossed the Nr2f2flox/flox allele with tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice (tip-cell-specific Nr2f2 deletion; hereafter, tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC mice) and optimized 4-OHT dosing to maximize recombination of both alleles (Fig. 5a). NR2F2 expression was efficiently reduced in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC retinas (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Deletion of Nr2f2 alone neither impaired mobilization of Esm1-traced Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC-GFP+ cells into arteries nor altered vascular density (Fig. 5b–d and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Importantly, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R cells to contribute to arteries (Fig. 5b,c), whereas endothelial hyperproliferation and vascular expansion remained essentially unchanged compared with tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice (Fig. 5d–f and Extended Data Fig. 10d).
