Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (c, d and f) and two-tailed unpaired t-tests (h). Scale bars, 200 μm (b) and 20 μm (e).

We confirmed these findings using the complementary tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R clonal tracing model (Extended Data Fig. 11a–i). Whereas Cherry+ and Cherry+ Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC endothelial cells contributed similarly to arteries, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells were detected in 35% of arteries, compared with 10% for eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells (Extended Data Fig. 11c,e). Moreover, most eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells that reached arteries did not form lesions, whereas eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells consistently generated small arterial lesions (Extended Data Fig. 11c,f). Nevertheless, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells continued to overexpand within the capillary plexus (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i). Together, these findings demonstrate that NR2F2 mediates the PIK3CA-driven block in arterial differentiation but is dispensable for mutant cell hyperproliferation in non-arterial vessels.

To investigate how PIK3CAH1047R activation induces NR2F2 expression, we analysed endothelial cells in culture. Nr2f2 transcript levels increased within 24 h after 4-OHT-induced recombination and remained elevated thereafter (Extended Data Fig. 12a). NR2F2 protein levels increased by 72 h (Extended Data Fig. 12b–d). To test whether Nr2f2 induction depends on PI3K signalling, endothelial cells were treated with the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719). PI3Kα inhibition reduced Nr2f2 mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, accompanied by reduced p-AKT levels (Extended Data Fig. 12e–h). Similarly, alpelisib reduced NR2F2 transcript and protein levels in patient-derived endothelial cells with activating PIK3CA mutations (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j).

Industry observers note that to investigate the transcriptional mechanisms underlying NR2F2 induction, we focused on FOXO transcription factors, major downstream effectors of PI3K signalling7,32, with FOXO1 the predominant family member in endothelial cells33. PI3K–AKT signalling inhibits FOXO1 through phosphorylation-dependent nuclear exclusion7,32 and, consistent with this, FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus in vascular lesions of Pik3caH1047R mutant mice (Extended Data Fig. 12k,l). We next examined whether FOXO1 directly regulates NR2F2. Analysis of published RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq), FOXO1 chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) and H3K27ac ChIP–seq datasets from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing constitutively nuclear, PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3)34,35 revealed sustained repression of NR2F2 transcripts and protein, reduced chromatin accessibility at the NR2F2 locus and FOXO1 binding to a vein-specific NR2F2 enhancer (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12m–v). FOXO1(A3) increased occupancy at this enhancer while reducing H3K27 acetylation and chromatin accessibility, consistent with direct transcriptional repression (Extended Data Fig. 12p).

Conversely, endothelial deletion of Foxo1 markedly increased Nr2f2 transcript and protein levels (Fig. 5h,i). Finally, induction of PIK3CAH1047R in HUVECs increased NR2F2 expression, whereas the PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3) suppressed this response (Fig. 5j). Together, these findings establish FOXO1 as a transcriptional repressor of NR2F2 and define a PI3K–FOXO1–NR2F2 axis through which oncogenic PIK3CA disrupts arterial differentiation.

Sources indicate that using the vasculature as a model, we show that the consequences of PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial cell context. Depending on the differentiation state of the affected endothelial cell, the mutation promotes pathological proliferation, remains phenotypically silent or disrupts differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 13). This context-dependent model provides a mechanistic explanation for the marked predominance of capillary and venous lesions, and the rarity of arterial lesions, in PIK3CA-driven vascular disease. More broadly, it may also help to explain why PIK3CA-associated overgrowth preferentially affects mesoderm-derived tissues and suggests that similar principles probably apply to other pathogenic PIK3CA variants, which exhibit comparable lesion distributions in patients3.

It has been revealed that genetic lineage tracing revealed that endothelial cells expressing endogenous Pik3caH1047R persist in mature arteries without eliciting a detectable phenotype. Consistently, embryonic expression of Pik3caH1047R in Tie2+ cells does not give rise to arterial lesions32. This finding is unexpected given the broad endothelial expression of Pik3ca and the prominent role of PI3Kα signalling in all endothelial cells33. However, basal PI3K signalling is comparatively low in arteries and is not increased by endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression. By contrast, forced overexpression, enhances PI3K signalling and induces mild overgrowth in arterial endothelial cells that have not yet completed differentiation, suggesting that these cells require higher signalling levels to mount a pathological response than venous or capillary endothelial cells. Nevertheless, increased PI3K signalling does not induce overgrowth or NR2F2 expression in fully differentiated arteries. Likewise, reducing shear stress or Notch signalling, key pathways in the acquisition and maintenance of arterial identity30,34,35, does not restore responsiveness to Pik3caH1047R. These findings suggest that arterial endothelial cells possess multiple layers of protection that may also underlie their broader resistance to other mutations36. Future studies are needed to determine how microenvironmental cues, including extracellular matrix composition and mural cell interactions, contribute to this resistance.

It has been revealed that we also find that PIK3CAH1047R disrupts arterial differentiation at early developmental stages. During angiogenesis, a subset of tip cells acquires a pre-arterial identity by expressing canonical arterial markers (such as CXCR4, UNC5B, HEY1 and DLL4)30,37,38 and migrates retrogradely into nascent arteries to support arterial expansion. Pik3caH1047R disrupts this transition by inducing an early hyperproliferation response followed by Nr2f2 upregulation and loss of arterial identity. Supporting a causal role for NR2F2, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R tip cells to contribute to arteries, consistent with previous studies demonstrating that NR2F2 antagonizes pre-arterial specification26. More broadly, our findings align with evidence that PI3K signalling promotes venous specification39,40, suppresses arterial differentiation41 and favours a stemness state42. Similar effects have been reported in other tissues, where PIK3CAH1047R biases ageing oesophageal progenitor cells towards self-renewal and induces dedifferentiation during mammary tumorigenesis14,15. In parallel, we show that proliferation blockade in Pik3caH1047R-expressing pre-arterial cells limits lesion formation, but neither reduces NR2F2 expression nor restores arterial contribution of mutant cells. These findings indicate that impaired arterial differentiation cannot be explained solely by proliferative exclusion43,44. Conversely, NR2F2 depletion did not block lesion growth or endothelial proliferation, despite previous reports implicating NR2F2 in cell cycle regulation25,45. Together, these findings indicate that PIK3CAH1047R-driven endothelial proliferation and the NR2F2-mediated arterial differentiation defect are functionally separable downstream outputs.

Our findings identify a transcriptional mechanism linking PI3K activation to NR2F2 induction. Previous studies demonstrated that TIE2–PI3K signalling stabilizes NR2F2 protein during venous specification39 and that NR2F2 is elevated in PI3K-driven prostate tumours46. We show that PI3K signalling also promotes NR2F2 transcript and protein expression by inhibiting FOXO1. This is consistent with the established role of FOXO factors as nuclear effectors of PI3K signalling, including in PIK3CA-related vascular malformations47, and with the vascular overgrowth caused by endothelial FOXO1 loss48. Notably, FOXO1 has been reported to promote NR2F2 transcript and protein expression in pancreatic β cells49, whereas our data identify FOXO1 as a direct NR2F2 repressor in endothelial cells. Although the molecular basis of this difference remains to be determined, it is consistent with the context-dependent transcriptional activity of FOXO factors and NR2F2 regulation50,51 and may reflect differences in enhancer use and FOXO1 occupancy. Given that additional transcription factors regulate endothelial NR2F2 expression52,53,54, defining how they cooperate with or compete with FOXO1 will help to explain this context-dependent regulation.

It has been revealed that together, our findings show that the pathological consequences of oncogenic PIK3CA activation depend not only on signalling strength but also on developmental state and endothelial identity. Differentiated arterial cells resist pathological overgrowth, whereas pre-arterial cells undergo an NR2F2-mediated differentiation defect alongside increased proliferation. These functionally separable responses help to explain the vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

The in vivo experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines and legislation of the Catalan Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries and Food (Catalonia, Spain), following protocols approved by the local animal experimentation ethics committee (CEEA) of the Institut Germans Trias i Pujol (IGTP) and local animal authorities of the State of Berlin (Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales Berlin). Mice were housed in individually ventilated cages under specific-pathogen-free conditions. All mice were crossed onto the C57BL/6J genetic background. Both male and female pups were used for retinal experiments.

The following mouse strains were used in this study. Pdgfb-creERT2-eGFP (pan-endothelial Cre line)55 mice were provided by M. Fruttiger. Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2 (pan-endothelial Cre line)56, Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 (arterial-endothelial Cre line)57 and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 (tip-endothelial Cre line)58 mice were obtained from R. Adams. The R26-mTmG59 mice express membrane-targeted Tomato in the absence of Cre activity and this switches to membrane-targeted GFP expression after Cre activation, enabling cell lineage visualization and tracking. Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, which harbour a Cre-inducible H1047R point mutation in the endogenous Pik3ca locus, were provided by W. Phillips60. In this allele, loxPsites flank exon 20, which is replaced after Cre recombination by a downstream version containing a CAT-to-AGG substitution at codon 1047. The two loxPsites are only 419 bp apart, making this region highly recombinogenic. Consistent with this, robust phenotypes are observed even at low doses of 4-OHT19. We occasionally observed vascular overgrowth in regions lacking GFP labelling, suggesting the presence of mutant cells in which the reporter allele had not recombined. Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R mice (hereafter iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) overexpress the human PIK3CAH1047R cDNA along with H2B-eGFP-V5 (details are provided in the next section and Extended Data Fig. 5). The Nr2f2flox/flox mouse line61, provided by S. Y. Tsai, was used for conditional deletion of Nr2f2. The Foxo1flox/flox mouse line62 was used for conditional deletion of Foxo1. A list of all mouse lines and genotyping primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

To induce CreERT2 activity in pups, 4-OHT (Sigma-Aldrich, H7905) was dissolved in ethanol to prepare a 10 mg ml−1 solution. The stock solution was aliquoted and stored at −20 °C. Pups received intragastric injections in volumes adjusted to deliver the doses specified in the figures. To achieve the desired recombination pattern (such as sparse mosaic recombination, efficient recombination or recombination of multiple alleles), the 4-OHT dose was titrated for each CreERT2 line and experimental configuration (Supplementary Table 2).

It has been revealed that to inhibit proliferation, pups received palbociclib (70 mg kg−1 in distilled H2O; Selleckchem S1116; intraperitoneal (i.p.), P3–P5) or mitomycin C (10 mg kg−1 in PBS, Sigma-Aldrich, M4287, i.p., P4–P5). To modulate blood flow and inhibit the Notch signalling pathway, pups received captopril (4.125 mg kg−1 in PBS; Sigma-Aldrich, C4042; i.p., P4–P5) or DAPT (100 mg kg−1 in DMSO/peanut oil; Calbiochem, 565770; subcutaneous, P4–P5). DAPT stock (10 mg ml−1) was prepared by dissolving 5 mg in 50 µl DMSO at 40 °C for 10 min and diluting in 450 µl peanut oil. To assess endothelial cell proliferation, pups were injected i.p. with 100 μg of EdU and euthanized 2 h later. EdU incorporated into the retina was detected using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 594 Imaging Kit (Invitrogen, C10339).

To generate the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R) mouse line, we introduced the DNA insert containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-humanPIK3CAH1047R gene by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homologous-dependent repair, in the previously targeted iChr2-Mosaic mouse embryonic stem (ES) cell line31. To generate the donor construct of interest, we first obtained the HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence from the plasmid pBabe-puro-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R (Addgene, 12524) and cloned it into plasmid SO107 (Addgene, 99617)31, which contained the LoxP2-H2B-eGFP-V5-2A cassette. We then inserted the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R cassette into the donor vector JP6 (Addgene, 99627), which contains the hygromycin-resistance gene. This resulted in the generation of the donor vector NA453, containing the complete donor construct of interest (Extended Data Fig. 5). ES cells of the G4 genetic background63 were cultured in standard ES cell medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with GlutaMax (31966-047, Gibco), 15% FBS (tested for germline transmission), 1× non-essential amino acids (Hyclone, SH3023801), 0.1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, M7522), 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Lonza, DE17-602E) and leukaemia inhibitory factor. ES cells were maintained on dishes coated with a feeder layer of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). For each nucleofection, 2.5 × 106 ES cells were resuspended in 100 µl nucleofection solution containing 1.5 µg of circular px330 plasmid (NA505), encoding the guide RNA sequence (Guide3, GTTGCCTATGAGAGGCTAGAC), and 3.5 µg circular donor plasmid (NA453) containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence and the PGK-hygromycin resistance cassette (Extended Data Fig. 5). After nucleofection, 5 µl or 30 µl of the cell suspension was plated into separate wells on a six-well plate containing MEF feeder layers. Then, 7 days after hygromycin selection, 24 isolated ES cell colonies were picked for cryopreservation and subsequent screening. PCR with the flanking primers identified clones with correct homologous recombination and targeted insertion. After identifying correctly targeted ES cell clones, the functionality of the targeted allele was validated by transient transfection of a Cre-expressing plasmid. Positive clones were expanded and microinjected into C57BL/6J host blastocysts. Chimeric mice with a high degree of agouti coat colour were subsequently bred to achieve germline transmission of the targeted allele.

Mice were euthanized by decapitation, and their eyes were isolated and incubated on ice in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Sigma-Aldrich, 158127) in PBS for 1 h. Retinas were dissected and fixed for an additional 1 h in 4% PFA on ice, washed three times in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C in blocking buffer (1% BSA, 3% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) with gentle agitation. For NR2F2 staining, retinas were subjected to antigen retrieval by boiling for 20 min in 0.01 M citrate buffer (pH 6, Sigma-Aldrich, W305600) before permeabilization. Retinas were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CA retinas, the antigen-retrieval step required for NR2F2 staining abolished the GFP signal and prevented detection with anti-GFP antibodies; therefore, the retinas were incubated overnight with anti-GFP antibodies before antigen retrieval. After washing three times in PBST (0.1% Tween-20 in PBS), the retinas were incubated for 30 min at room temperature in PBLEC buffer (1% Triton X-100, 1 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM MnCl2 in PBS (pH 6.8)). Secondary Alexa-Fluor-conjugated antibodies or isolectin GS-B4 (IB4) were incubated with retinas in PBLEC buffer for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. After three additional washes with PBST, retinas were flat-mounted onto microscope slides with Mowiol (Calbiochem, 475904), supplemented with the anti-fade reagent DABCO (1.4-diazabicyclo-(2.2.2)octane; Sigma-Aldrich, D27802) or Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For FOXO1/ERG co-immunostaining, an additional blocking step was included because both primary antibodies were raised in the same species, thereby preventing cross-reactivity. After the incubation with the anti-FOXO1 antibody and its corresponding secondary antibody, retinas were incubated with AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragments donkey anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-006-152, 1:100) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. The retinas were then washed, briefly fixed with 4% PFA, blocked again and incubated with the primary Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated anti-ERG antibody. A list of all of the primary and secondary antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Mouse endothelial cells were isolated from the lungs of adult mice (both female and male) aged 3 to 6 weeks. Under sterile conditions, lungs were minced and digested in 4 U ml−1 dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14170-112) for 1 h at 37 °C with constant agitation. Tissue was further dissociated by pipetting to obtain a single-cell suspension, and digestion was stopped with Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Biowest, S1810-500) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15140-122). Cells were resuspended in PBS and incubated for 30 min at room temperature with rat anti-CD144 (Cdh5; BD Biosciences, 55289) antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 11035). CD144+ cells were washed in PBS containing 0.5% BSA and sorted by magnetic separation. CD144+ cells were plated on 0.5% gelatine-coated 12-well plates (Sigma-Aldrich, G1890) and cultured in complete DMEM/F12 (PromoCell, C-30140) supplemented with 20% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and two vials of endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H; PromoCell, C-30120). Once confluent, a second selection with CD144-antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads was performed for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were trypsinized, magnet-sorted, resuspended in F12 complete medium and cultured in a six-well format. Cells were maintained at 37 °C under a 5% CO2 atmosphere and used for experiments up to passage 5. Primary cells were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. Mouse endothelial cells used in Fig. 5i,j were isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox lungs as described previously64.

It has been revealed that to induce CreERT2-mediated recombination in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 5 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, and cultured for a further 72 h. Then, 1 day before immunofluorescence analysis, cells were replated at low confluency onto gelatine-coated coverslips in 12-well plates. At 4 h before collection, the culture medium was replaced with starvation medium, after which cells were processed for immunofluorescence. For mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2-Pik3caH1047R/+ mice, recombination was induced by treatment with 2 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, followed by the indicated experimental conditions before collection for immunoblot or qPCR analysis. For mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox mice, recombination was induced with 250 nM 4-OHT or vehicle control (DMSO), and cells were analysed 72 h after treatment.

It has been revealed that pooled HUVECs were purchased from Lonza (CC-2519) and cultured in EBM endothelial cell growth basal medium (EBM, Lonza, CC-3121) supplemented with EGM endothelial cell growth medium SingleQuots kit (Lonza, CC-4133) and 10% FBS (Life Technologies). Human embryonic kidney (HEK293FT) cells were used to produce lentiviruses and purchased from Life Technologies (R70007). HEK293FT cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, 31966-021) supplemented with 10% FBS (Life Technologies) and gentamicin (500 µg ml−1, Lonza, 17-518L). Cells were purchased from commercial suppliers, visually inspected for expected morphology and used for a limited number of passages. No further authentication was performed in-house. All cells were tested negative for mycoplasma and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2.

Recent findings suggest that for doxycycline-inducible lentiviral expression of PIK3CAH1047R, a V5-PIK3CAH1047R-encoding cDNA was cloned into the pLVX-TetOne-Puro vector (Takara, 631847). For CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing, gene-specific gRNA sequences (Supplementary Table 4) were cloned into a plentiCRISPRv2 plasmid co-expressing Flag-tagged Cas9 nuclease and a puromycin-selection marker (Addgene, 52961). Lentivirus production was performed by co-transfection of HEK293FT cells with pMD2.G (Addgene, 12259), psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260) and transfer plasmids. Transfections were performed using the Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Life Technologies, 11668027) as previously described65. Viruses were collected 48 and 72 h after transfection and filtered through a 0.45-μm filter. HUVECs were transduced with lentiviruses for 16 h in the presence of 8 μg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220) and selected with 1 μg ml−1 puromycin (InvivoGen, ant-pr-1). Lentiviral expression of PIK3CAH1047R was induced by stimulating HUVECs with 600 ng ml−1 doxycycline (Sigma-Aldrich, D9891) for 72 h.

In a recent development, subconfluent HUVECs were transduced with custom-made adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs) to overexpress constitutively nuclear human FOXO1 (FOXO1A3-Flag) or control (CMV-null) adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs, 1300). For adenoviral transductions, HUVECs were incubated in EBM medium (Lonza, CC-3121) containing 0.1% (v/v) BSA (Sigma-Aldrich, 1595) for 4 h and transduced with the respective viruses for an additional 4 h in the presence of 8 µg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220). HUVECs were then washed five times with Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14175095) and cultured for the indicated times in EBM basal medium supplemented with 10% FBS and EGM SingleQuots.

Sources indicate that gene-specific gRNA sequences to target the NR2F2-1345 enhancer were designed using CHOPCHOP66. For each target gene, we used three independent gRNAs and co-transfected them with packaging vectors for lentivirus production. After transduction, puromycin was used to select a pool of CRISPR–Cas9-mediated mutant HUVECs. The knockout efficiency was confirmed by PCR analysis of gDNA isolated from transduced cells. Single guide RNA sequences and genotyping primers are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

Cells were washed with warm 1% PBS containing Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Gibco, 14080-055), fixed for 15 min in 4% PFA and washed again with warm PBS. For staining, cells were permeabilized for 5 min with 0.4% Triton X-100 in PBS, followed by a 1 h incubation in blocking buffer (2% BSA in PBS). After washing with PBS, cells were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. Subsequently, secondary AlexaFluor-conjugated antibodies were diluted in blocking buffer and added to the cells for a 1 h incubation at room temperature. After additional washes with PBS, cells were incubated with DAPI (Invitrogen, D1305; 1:500) for 1 min and then mounted on microscope slides with Fluoromount-G (Southern Biotech, 0100-01). A list of all of the antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Recent findings suggest that human endothelial cells were isolated from patient biopsies of vascular malformations. These biopsies were obtained during therapeutic surgical resection, with informed consent and approval from the Biomedical Committees at Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, Hospital Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge and Hospital Universitario Germans Trias i Pujol (codes PR264/16, PIC-96-16 and PI-21-171). Experiments adhered to the WMA Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report. Data were stored in a secure database maintained by Hospital Sant Joan de Deu. Biopsies were homogenized and digested in dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) and collagenase A (Roche Diagnostics, 10103586001) for up to 1.5 h at 37 °C, with continuous movement. The tissue was dissociated by pipetting into a single-cell solution, then inactivated with DMEM (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin). Cells were resuspended in 0.5% BSA in PBS and incubated with CD31-antibody-coated (Agilent Dako, M0823, JC70A) magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11041) for 1 h at room temperature. The CD31+ fraction was magnetically sorted, resuspended and cultured in 0.5% gelatine-coated wells in EGM2 medium (PromoCell, C-39211) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin (EGM2 complete) at 37 °C and 5% CO2 until confluency. Cells were then subjected to a second CD31-based magnetic selection. Mycoplasma testing was not performed on primary cells. To validate the presence of the mutation in isolated endothelial cells, genomic DNA was extracted according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, K182001) and detected by next-generation sequencing. For the vascular malformation (VM) 64, we obtained from 1,572 reads, c.3140A>G (H1047R) with a 45.86% variant allelic frequency and for the VM90 from 461 reads, c.2740A>G (E545G) with 48.37% variant allelic frequency.

It has been revealed that cells were lysed in ice-cold lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 5 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl and 1% Triton X-100, supplemented with protease (Roche, 11836153001) and phosphatase (Sigma-Aldrich, 4906837001) inhibitors. The protein concentration was measured using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Total cell lysates were resolved on 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gels using a Mini-Protean Tetra Vertical Electrophoresis Cell (Bio-Rad, 1658004) and subsequently transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes using a Mini Trans-Blotcell system (Bio-Rad, 1703930). Membranes were blocked with 5% milk in TBST (TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20) and incubated with appropriate primary antibodies diluted in 2% BSA in TBST. Secondary antibodies were diluted in 5% milk in TBST. Immunoblots were visualized using ECL (0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 9.35, 2.2 mM luminol, 2.2 mM p-coumaric acid and 0.06% H2O2). Western blots shown in Fig. 5i,j and Extended Data Fig. 12o,s were performed as described previously65. Information on all antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3. Uncropped western blot images are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2.

Recent findings suggest that RNA was extracted using the Maxwell RSC SimplyRNA Cells Kit (Promega, AS1390) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and RNA quality was assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Reverse transcription was performed using 500 ng of RNA from cell lysate samples with the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, 4368814). qPCR was performed using a QuantStudio 7 Flex system with SYBR Green real-time PCR master mix (Applied Biosystems, A46110). RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis and qPCR for Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12n,r,u were performed as previously described65. Primer sequences and TaqMan assay IDs are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

To inhibit PI3Kα activity, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated with ethanol or 4-OHT for 6 h, followed by vehicle or the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719; at 1 or 5 µM) for an additional 66 h. Patient-derived endothelial cells isolated from venous malformations were treated with vehicle or BYL719 (1 µM or 5 µM) for 72 h before downstream analysis. To inhibit proliferation in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were cultured for 24 h in DMEM/F12 supplemented with reduced growth factors (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H)) to limit baseline proliferation and achieve approximately 40% confluency. Cells were then treated with palbociclib (2 μM) or vehicle (PBS), followed 6 h later by the addition of 4-OHT (2 μM) or ethanol while maintaining palbociclib treatment. Cells were collected 24 h after 4-OHT treatment for western blot, qPCR analysis and flow cytometry.

Sources indicate that for EdU incorporation assays, EdU (10 μM) was added 2 h before collection. Cells were processed using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 647 Flow Cytometry Assay Kit (Invitrogen, C10634) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data were acquired on a BD FACSymphony A1 cell analyser and analysed using FlowJo (v.10.1, BD Biosciences). Cells were gated based on forward and side scatter to exclude debris and doublets before analysis as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3.

In a recent development, imaging was performed with Leica Stellaris 8, Leica TCS SP5, Zeiss LSM 980 and Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscopes, operated with LAS X v.4.8.2, LAS AF v.2.7 and Zen v.3.9 software, respectively. Adobe Photoshop (v.25.12.0), Adobe Illustrator (64-bit, v.29.0.1), ImageJ v.1.54b, CellProfiler v.4.2.6 and Imaris v.10.1 were used for image processing and quantification. All images shown in the figures are maximum intensity projections. Images were taken from at least three retinal areas in each retina and are representative of at least four retinas analysed for each genotype unless otherwise stated. The identification of retinal vascular lesions and their locations was performed by observing IB4 in ×10 images. Vascular malformations were defined based on abnormal vessel morphology and GFP+ clonal expansion. In capillary beds, lesions were identified as focal regions displaying abnormal vessel enlargement compared with the surrounding capillary plexus and associated clusters of GFP+ endothelial cells. In veins and arteries, malformations were defined by the presence of GFP+ endothelial cell clusters indicative of clonal expansion, together with abnormal vessel enlargement compared with control vessels. Retinal vascularity was measured using the IB4 channel by adjusting the threshold to select IB4+, followed by quantification of the percentage of IB4+ area relative to the total retinal surface. Vessel width was determined by measuring the average diameter at three different points along each vessel. GFP+ cell expansion was quantified by calculating the percentage of GFP+ area within the IB4+ area. For capillary analysis, images containing only capillary beds were used. To quantify GFP+ cells in veins and arteries, IB4 staining was used to delineate the vascular area, and vessel-specific regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to arteries or veins were manually selected. For quantification of aEC-GFP+ endothelial cells, the analysed area was defined by a fixed ROI (200 × 550 μm (P6 retinas), 200 × 630 μm (P9 retinas) and 500 × 1,200 μm (P12 retinas)) to maintain consistent arterial length across replicates and to avoid including other vascular types. In P21 retinas, aEC-GFP+ cells were spread across various vessel types, so the ROI for quantification included the entire vascular plexus. To quantify vascular p-S6 intensity, a manual threshold was set to obtain the GFP+ area and define the ROI. The integrated density of p-S6 was then measured within the GFP+ area. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice, p-S6 integrated density was quantified separately in Cherry+ (WT) or eGFP+ (PIK3CAH1047R) cells after manual delineation of IB4+ areas containing each recombinant cell population. In both cases, the background signal (mean grey values) was measured in adjacent IB4-negative regions. The corrected total fluorescence (CTF) was calculated using the following equation: CTF = integrated density – (vascular area × mean grey background value). αSMA, CX37 and UNC5B expression in endothelial cells was quantified by measuring the mean intensity within GFP+ areas. Endothelial cell proliferation was quantified as the percentage of ERG+ endothelial cell nuclei co-immunostained positive for Ki-67 or EdU relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. In the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, proliferation was quantified separately for Cherry+ and eGFP+ nuclei as the percentage of Ki-67+ nuclei relative to the total number of Cherry+ or eGFP+ nuclei, respectively. Nuclear FOXO1 positivity was quantified as the percentage of FOXO1+ERG+ nuclei relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. NR2F2 levels were assessed by manual scoring of nuclear immunofluorescence intensity in ERG+ endothelial cells. Endothelial nuclei with strong and unequivocal nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2high, nuclei with weak but discernible nuclear signal as NR2F2low and nuclei lacking detectable nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2negative, including after a substantial increase in display intensity during image visualization. Scoring was performed using identical acquisition settings across samples. Quantification of Cherry+ and eGFP+ endothelial cells in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was performed manually, differentiating their presence in capillaries, veins and arteries. Vascular lesions were classified based on size as small (<10 PIK3CAH1047R cells), medium (between 10 and 35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) or large (>35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) based on manual counting of PIK3CAH1047R mutant cells. The incidence of arteries populated with PIK3CAH1047R cells was determined as a percentage in relation to the total number of arteries containing any recombinant cell. The relative arterial vessel width in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was assessed by comparing vessel diameter in a central region containing recombinant cells with adjacent regions of the same vessel lacking recombinant cells.

Sources indicate that in cultured endothelial cells, maximum-intensity projections of confocal images were analysed using CellProfiler (v.4.2.6). DAPI, eGFP, Cherry and Ki-67 signals were defined as primary objects. Nuclei were identified based on DAPI staining and used to generate secondary objects for p-S6 quantification. CellProfiler assigned p-S6 intensity to individual nuclei and classified cells as p-S6+ or p-S6−. WT and PIK3CAH1047R endothelial cells were quantified by identifying Cherry+DAPI+ and eGFP+DAPI+ cells, respectively.

In a recent development, FOXO1-bound Nr2f2 enhancer identification was performed according an approach described previously67. In brief, enhancer marks from three published datasets were used to identify putative enhancers: (1) open chromatin as assessed by ATAC–seq in mouse P6 retina endothelial cells (MRECs)68; (2) enriched EP300 binding in Tie2-cre+ cells from embryonic day 11.5 mouse embryos69; and (3) binding of the ETS factor ERG, which marks all known endothelial cell enhancers, in HUVECs70. Putative enhancer regions were then assessed for FOXO1(A3) binding47,65, identifying the FOXO1-bound NR2F2-1345 enhancer. For in vivo validation, the NR2F2-1345 enhancer sequence was cloned into the E1b-GFP-Tol2-Gateway vector71 using the Gene Synthesis service from Genewiz (part of Azenta Life Sciences). F0 mosaic transgenic zebrafish embryos were generated using Tol2-mediated integration72. All animal procedures were approved by a local ethical review committee at Oxford University, licensed by the UK Home Office and conducted in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. All zebrafish (KLC strain) were maintained in groups. Embryos were maintained in E3 medium (5 mM NaCl, 0.17 mM KCl, 0.33 mM CaCl2, 0.33 mM MgSO4) at 28.5 °C. To image, all embryos were dechorionated and anaesthetized with 0.01% tricaine methanesulfonate in E3 medium. For analysis of transgenic zebrafish, single embryos were transferred into a flat-bottom 96-well plate, mounted in 0.1% TopVision low-melting-point agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R0801) in E3 medium with tricaine methanesulfonate (Merck, A5040). GFP reporter gene expression was screened with a Zeiss LSM 980 (Carl Zeiss) confocal microscope at 32–72 h post-fertilization. Whole zebrafish were imaged using the ‘tile scan’ command, combined with z-stack collection, at 488 nm excitation and 510 nm emission for eGFP.

In a recent development, to target tip endothelial cells, recombination was induced with 25 mg kg−1 4-OHT at P1 and P2 in Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG (control) and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG;Pik3caH1047R (mutant) mice. Retinas were collected at P6 and processed fresh for enzymatic dissociation using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-092-628). After dissociation, the cell suspension was incubated with CD31 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-097-418) and subjected to two consecutive rounds of magnetic separation using MS columns (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-201) and an OctoMACS Separator (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-109). Cells were resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS and processed for scRNA-seq using the 10x Genomics platform. Two independent experiments were performed on separate days using independent cohorts of control and mutant mice, with retinas pooled per genotype (Exp1: n = 5 control, n = 3 mutant; Exp2: n = 4 control, n = 4 mutant).

According to recent reports, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated in vitro overnight with 2 μM 4-OHT to induce recombination and expression of Pik3caH1047R, while ethanol-treated cells were used as a control (WT cells for Pik3ca). The medium was then changed to F12 complete, and cells were collected 48 h post-induction. Cells were detached with trypsin, centrifuged, subjected to debris removal (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-109-398) and finally resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS. For the scRNA-seq, three independent biological replicates were pooled for each treatment condition.

Single cells were encapsulated into emulsion droplets using the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics) with the 3′ Next GEM kit (v3 chemistry) or the Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Kit v4 for in vitro and in vivo samples, respectively. Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s protocol, targeting a recovery of around 10,000 cells per sample. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq X 25B platform using 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads. Raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger (v.7.0.1 or v.8.0.1) and aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) using the default parameters. For the in vivo datasets, raw UMI count matrices were corrected for ambient RNA contamination using CellBender (v.0.2.1)73. This approach models background RNA from empty droplets and infers corrected expression counts for cell-containing droplets using a probabilistic framework. Corrected matrices were used for downstream analyses.

According to recent reports, all scRNA-seq datasets (in vivo and in vitro) were processed using a unified analytical pipeline in R (v.4.2.2) with the Seurat package (v.4.9.9)74. CellBender output count matrices were imported using a custom function designed to read H5AD files in R. Each sample was initially processed independently. tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were initially analysed separately to prevent the pronounced transcriptional changes associated with the mutation from dominating the global data structure and obscuring the physiological organization of the tEC-GFP retina. After independent quality control, dimensionality reduction and clustering, endothelial cells were identified within each genotype based on canonical marker expression. The endothelial subsets from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were subsequently combined and jointly reanalysed to enable direct comparison of endothelial states across genotypes while retaining an accurate representation of the WT retinal vasculature. Within each condition, control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells and uninformative genes. Cells were excluded if they contained fewer than 250 detected genes, more than 20% mitochondrial transcripts or exhibited a complexity index greater than 0.8. Genes with zero counts across all cells were removed. Potential doublets were estimated using DoubletFinder (v.2.0.3) on a per-sample basis75. Although doublets were not removed from the dataset, they were excluded from downstream differential expression analyses. Data normalization was performed using Seurat’s NormaliseData function with the LogNormalise method and a scale factor of 10,000. Highly variable genes (HVGs) were defined based on the distribution of non-zero gene expression counts, selecting a threshold corresponding to the third quartile plus 100 genes. Data were then scaled using ScaleData, and then a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using RunPCA. To correct for batch effects across biological replicates, datasets were integrated using the Harmony algorithm (v.1.2.3)76, applied to PCA embeddings. The sample identity (ID) was used as the batch variable, enabling alignment of cells across replicates while preserving biological variability. Harmony-corrected principal components were used for downstream analyses. Graph-based clustering was performed by constructing a shared-nearest-neighbour graph using FindNeighbours, followed by community detection with the Louvain algorithm implemented in FindClusters. To specifically analyse the vascular compartment, endothelial cells were identified based on canonical marker expression (Pecam1 and Cdh5) and computationally subsetted. A secondary, endothelial-focused analysis pipeline was then applied, including re-identification of highly variable features, normalization, scaling, PCA and Harmony integration76. Multiple clustering resolutions (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5) were evaluated, with a resolution of 0.3 selected as it best recapitulated known endothelial cell subpopulations (for example, tip, arterial, venous and proliferative endothelial cells). Cluster annotation was performed using a one-versus-all differential expression approach with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers function, applying the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.

According to recent reports, in the in vivo retinal endothelial cell dataset, GFP expression was used to identify recombined endothelial cells. To enable GFP quantification, the GFP coding sequence was appended to the standard mouse reference genome (mm10), and raw sequencing reads were aligned against this modified reference using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger v.8.0.1. This allowed simultaneous quantification of endogenous transcripts and GFP expression. To identify GFP-expressing cells, GFP transcript levels were examined across the dataset. Density plots of log-normalized GFP expression revealed a bimodal distribution, which enabled the application of a stringer classification threshold (log-normalized expression > 1.5). Cells with log-normalized GFP expression of greater than 1.5 were classified as GFP+, whereas cells with expression at or below this threshold were classified as GFP−.

Differential expression analysis was performed by comparing mutant (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R) and WT (GFP+ WT) cells within defined endothelial cell populations using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test implemented in Seurat (FindMarkers). To enhance robustness and account for sparsity inherent to single-cell data, a complementary pseudobulk approach was applied. Raw counts were aggregated at the sample level (grouped by ID and phenotype) using AggregateExpression, treating each mouse as an independent biological replicate. The resulting count matrix was analysed using DESeq2 (v.1.38.3)77, applying a generalized linear model based on the negative binomial distribution. Concordance between single-cell and pseudobulk approaches was assessed by correlating log2[FC] values across clusters and evaluating overlap of significantly regulated genes (adjusted P < 0.05). A high level of agreement in both magnitude and direction of gene regulation was observed. Based on this consistency, Wilcoxon-derived results were used for downstream visualization and functional analyses due to their higher sensitivity, while pseudobulk results served as an independent validation of biological signal.

Industry observers note that average expression profiles were calculated for each endothelial population using Seurat’s AverageExpression function and HVG. The 1,500 most variable genes were scaled by gene and hierarchically clustered using Pearson correlation distance and average linkage. Analyses included either all endothelial cells from tEC-GFP retinas, irrespective of GFP status, or only traced GFP+ endothelial cells from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R retinas. In the latter, populations were additionally stratified by genotype. Heat maps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.15.4).

To control for potential biases from unequal cell numbers between conditions (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R versus GFP+ WT), we implemented a bootstrapped downsampling strategy. For each endothelial cell subtype, 1,000 iterations of random subsampling were performed. In each iteration, the condition with more cells was downsampled to match the size of the smaller group, thereby generating balanced datasets. Differential expression was recalculated in each iteration using the Wilcoxon test (FindMarkers, with logfc.threshold = 0 and min.pct = 0). For each gene, the frequency of significance (adjusted P < 0.05) and the consistency of log2[FC] direction were recorded across iterations. This approach confirmed that the identified transcriptional signatures were stable and reproducible, supporting their interpretation as robust biological features of the mutant phenotype rather than artefacts driven by differences in cell numbers.

According to recent reports, the expression of Nr2f2 and proliferation scores across GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells were estimated. Cell cycle and proliferation scores (the sum of S and G2/M phases) were computed using ccAFv278. Biological thresholds were established: the Nr2f2 threshold was set at the 99th percentile of reference WT arterial and artery capillary cells, and proliferation status used a cut-off of 0.1. Cells were categorized into Nr2f2 status, proliferation status and a joint status (double high, Nr2f2 high, proliferation high or low/basal).

RNA velocity was inferred with scVelo in GFP+ endothelial cells and further analysed using CellRank v.2. GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R cells were analysed independently using identical parameters. For each genotype, 2,000 highly variable genes were selected, and genotype-specific neighbourhood graphs and expression moments were calculated using 30 principal components and 15 neighbours. Transcriptional dynamics and velocities were estimated using the dynamical model. CellRank was subsequently used to construct a velocity-based transition matrix using the VelocityKernel and to identify macrostates using GPCCA. Velocity vectors were projected onto the shared integrated UMAP and visualized as streamlines and cell-level arrows.

Recent findings suggest that statistical analysis was performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad). Data are presented as the mean ± s.e.m. For in vivo experiments, each retina was considered an independent experimental unit. At least three mice from at least two independent litters were used per condition, except for in Extended Data Fig. 11i (n = 2). For the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, only retinas containing identified recombined cells were included. Experiments using mouse endothelial cells included biological replicates, whereas those using human endothelial cells were performed as independent experimental repeats. Sample sizes are indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance between two groups was assessed using either an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests or the two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test or two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s test was used. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample sizes; sample sizes were based on previous experiments. Reproducibility was confirmed through multiple independent experiments. The experiments were not randomized, and the investigators were not blinded during the experiments or data analysis.

a, Schematic of retinal vasculature. Veins (V) are shown in blue, arteries (A) in red, the capillary network in grey, and the sprouting front in green. b, Schematic of transgenic mouse strategy combining the pan-endothelial (pEC) tamoxifen-inducible Cre allele (Pdgfb-creERT2) with the Pik3caH1047R allele (pEC-Pik3caH1047R). c, Experimental timeline for studies using the Pdgfb-creERT2 mouse line. d, Confocal images of P6 control (Cre-negative) and pEC-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (grey). e, High-magnification confocal images of P6 control and pEC-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (grey). f, Quantification of vessel width in capillaries, veins and arteries (n = 6, 8, 6, 7, 6 and 7 retinas, left to right). g, Confocal images of P4 pEC-GFP and pEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan). h, High-magnification confocal images of P4 pEC-GFP and pEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas immunostained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan), ERG (blue, endothelial cell nuclei), and Ki-67 (yellow, proliferating cells). i, Quantification of ERG+Ki-67+ nuclei as proportion of total ERG+ nuclei within GFP+ areas (n = 8 and 9 retinas, left to right). Data are mean ± SEM. Two-tailed Mann-Whitney test (f,i). Scale bars, 150 μm (d,g), 30 μm (e) and 20 μm (h). V, veins; A, arteries (a,d,e).

It has been revealed that a, Schematic illustrating the effects of PIK3CAH1047R in distinct endothelial cell subtypes. Stochastic and mosaic expression of PIK3CAH1047R in venous and capillary endothelial cells drives clonal expansion and vascular overgrowth, whereas mature arterial endothelial cells remain largely refractory. Expression in tip/pre-arterial endothelial cells alters cell fate, impairing arterial differentiation and promoting a venous-like identity. b, Schematic summarizing the two main pathogenic consequences of PIK3CAH1047R activation: increased endothelial proliferation, which drives vascular overgrowth, and impaired arterial differentiation through PI3K-AKT-dependent FOXO1 nuclear exclusion and consequent upregulation of NR2F2. Parts of this schematic were created using BioRender; Graupera, M. https://BioRender.com/z9zj46a (2026).

By JAKE FENNER, US SPORTS WRITER and DAN MATTHEWS.

Published: 22:24 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 07:55 EST, 25 November 2026.

United States women's soccer star Trinity Rodman has backed out of an upcoming tournament hours after reports revealed she is no longer in a relationship with tennis star Ben Shelton.

Rodman was set to take part in the 2026 CONCACAF W Championship window in Texas, but has now pulled out due to what US Soccer called 'a minor shoulder injury' in a statement announcing the roster move.

According to recent reports, the statement notes the injury occurred during the 2026 NWSL Championship Game last Saturday, where Rodman and the Washington Spirit fell 2-1 to the Kansas City Current. US Soccer has replaced Rodman with Gotham FC winger Jaedyn Shaw.

Rodman's removal comes hours after the Daily Mail was first to report on her split from the American tennis star.

The American sporting couple began dating around March 2025, frequently supporting one another at their various events, but have recently decided to call time on their relationship.

It has been revealed that their conflicting work schedules and constant travel made it too challenging for the couple to continue maintaining their relationship, the Daily Mail understands. However, the pair are believed to remain close, despite their split.

American soccer stat Trinity Rodman has backed out of the USWNT roster for the 2026 CONCACAF W Championship taking place beginning later this week.

The announcement comes hours after the Daily Mail was first to report her split from longtime boyfriend and tennis star Ben Shelton.

US Soccer notes Rodman suffered 'a minor shoulder injury' in the 2026 NWSL Championship.

The couple were frequently forced to maintain their romance over long distance with Shelton constantly traveling around the globe while playing on the ATP Tour.

Despite multiple sacrifices and last-minute trips to attend each other's matches, it appears they could no longer make it work.

The Daily Mail has reached out to both Shelton and Rodman's representatives for comment.

Shelton, 24, suffered defeat in the semi-final of the ATP Finals on Saturday, losing 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-1) to Carlos Alcaraz in Turin, Italy.

The same evening, Rodman, 24, and the Washington Spirit lost the NWSL final to the KC Current.

The following evening, the American tennis star was spotted at Madison Square Garden for the Newly introduced York Knicks' game against the Indiana Pacers without Rodman, instead sitting on Celebrity Row alongside a friend and actress Inde Navarette.

The couple first went public with their relationship in March 2025 following speculation from fans.

Mystery surrounded the early stages of their relationship, as they initially dropped a playful hint as part of a TikTok trend last March then 'hard debuted' their romance soon afterwards.

Their conflicting work schedules made it too challenging to maintain their relationship.

The sporting power couple went public with their relationship around March 2025.

Rodman was a near-permanent fixture in Shelton's box throughout the US Open in September.

The USWNT star and the Spirit had played an NWSL game in Washington on the day of the final but Rodman left the capital almost immediately after the final whistle to make the mad dash to Upcoming York for Shelton's final.

The forward was captured crying inside Arthur Ashe Stadium in the wake of her boyfriend's loss to Alexander Zverev.

Rodman, the daughter of NBA legend Dennis Rodman, had cheered on the World No 4 at multiple other events, making her Wimbledon debut in May 2025.

Meanwhile, the tennis superstar was every bit the supportive boyfriend when he consoled Rodman after her team lost the NWSL championship game last November.

The World No 4 attended the Knicks game on Sunday, one day after losing the ATP semifinal.

Rodman and the Washington Spirit lost the NWSL Championship to the KC Current on Saturday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's newly introduced album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Recent findings suggest that biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he reveals little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

According to recent reports, in his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

It has been revealed that this outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

It has been revealed that wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Industry observers note that just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly noted in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Industry observers note that yet Biermann has mentioned his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

In a recent development, yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

Industry observers note that I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

Sources indicate that in a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

According to recent reports, afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he mentioned.

According to recent reports, he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he noted. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

According to recent reports, the singer-songwriter prepares to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

In a recent development, and should he ever die, he mentioned, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

According to recent reports, has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

Industry observers note that after leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

Industry observers note that the first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

In a recent development, following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

According to recent reports, sunderland at the moment find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

It has been revealed that speaking in his preview, Farke remarked: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”.

  • Manchester City fans have expressed concern over Erling Haaland's despondent interview following their Champions League draw with Napoli, with the star admitting he is 'questioning everything' amid their slump in form.
  • Enzo Maresca's side rescued a late draw at the Etihad on Tuesday night, with Rayan Cherki equalising in the 86th minute to secure a 2-2 draw with Napoli.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 04:06 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 08:33 EST, 25 November 2026.

Manchester City fans have expressed concern over Erling Haaland's despondent interview following their Champions League draw with Napoli, with the star admitting he is 'questioning everything' amid their slump in form.

Enzo Maresca's side rescued a late draw at the Etihad on Tuesday night, with Rayan Cherki equalising in the 86th minute to secure a 2-2 draw with Napoli.

The result, however, continued an underwhelming run of form with Man City having won just twice in their last seven matches – one of which was achieved in a penalty shoot-out against Brighton in the Carabao Cup.

Man City have suffered defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest in the Premier League in the run, as well as drawing with Fulham on the weekend.

Haaland, who captained Man City against Napoli, admitted post-match to TNT Sports that their underwhelming form has left the squad questioning themselves.

'We were not able to control and attack the game in the way we want,' Haaland said. 'Football is easy and difficult. When you win it's easy and you know what to do. When you don't you start questioning everything.

Erling Haaland cut a despondent figure as he admitted to 'questioning everything' after Man City's draw with Napoli continued their underwhelming form.

🗣️ "I have no idea what we were missing. You could feel it in the last few games that there's something that's not clicking fully."@Erling reflects on @ManCity's 2-2 draw with Napoli.🎤 @AndyKerrtv #UCL | #ManCity pic.twitter.com/Cx2Hzieom3.

'The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy.

'We have so much quality so it's about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.'.

Haaland admitted in another interview with Bein Sports that the run of form 'hurts', with the star having offered a resigned laugh when asked whether the draw against Napoli should be considered a 'good point'.

The 26-year-old was seen looking down throughout the minute and a half interview, while he also rubbed his face with his hand as he looked to find answers for Man City's recent struggles.

'How the game was we managed to come back two times, but we demand more,' Haaland said.

'We have to do better and find some ways to control the game more and perform in a better way.

'I have no idea what we were missing. You could feel it in the last few games that it is not clicking fully and we have to find out, stay positive and get the best out of every single day.

Sources indicate that 'With and without the armband I feel huge responsibility because all I want to do is perform for this club and win games for Man City and right now we are not doing that. It hurts.'.

Fans promptly noted Haaland's downbeat responses to questions and despondent body language during the interview.

Man City fans have expressed concerns over Haaland's downbeat responses and body language in the interview.

Fans claimed they have never seen Haaland 'looking this flat' and suggested the star 'looks distraught' amid their underwhelming run.

Recent findings suggest that 'I've never seen Haaland looking this flat. Not even close to it,' one commented.

Recent findings suggest that 'At least he’s being honest with himself. Looks distraught,' a second said, with a third writing 'Extremely concerning.'.

Recent findings suggest that 'Never seen Erling Haaland look like this before,' another added, while a Man City fan wrote 'You can really tell how confused Haaland is from his expression. They don’t have confidence in their own football.'.

One went as far as claiming 'Haaland looks like he’s done with Manchester City…' while sharing footage of his reaction to one of Napoli's goals on the night.

Other fans questioned whether Haaland and his Man City team-mates' recent slump may be related to concerns over the potential punishment the club could face for breaching financial rules.

Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing when the verdict was released in September. The club have since appealed.

An independent commission ruled Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period with ‘sham’ deals.

Man City were found to have artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules.

Man City have continued to insist they had 'irrefutable evidence' proving their innocence, but if the club loses its appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion.

Man City face Arsenal in a crucial match on Sunday as they look to make inroads in the Gunners six point lead at the top of the Premier League.

Haaland had pushed back against suggestions the case had affected their form during the international break, while stressing he was committed long-term to the club.

The forward's first answer to Norwegian broadcaster TV2 had spanned two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges after he was asked about the club's situation.

'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland noted.

'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle….

Industry observers note that 'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.'.

He continued: 'It's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it.

'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it.

'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.

The Man City star, who signed a nine-and-a-half-year contract in late 2024, told Norwegian television earlier this month that his focus was on helping the team to turn their form around.

The draw against Napoli leaves Man City lying sixth in the Champions League table - which would be enough to see Maresca's side to qualify for the last-16.

Man City face a crucial clash on the weekend when they face reigning champions Arsenal in the Premier League, as they look to halve the six-point gap to the leaders at the top of the table.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy mentioned US peace envoys asked whether Kyiv would withdraw from its eastern region of ‌Donbas ⁠in exchange ⁠for joining NATO, according to remarks to the media published on Saturday.

The suggestion was made following the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi to bring Russia's nearly 5-year war in Ukraine to a close.

The Ukrainian leader told reporters: "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would ⁠Ukraine ​withdraw from Donbas?'".

According to recent reports, zelenskyy repeated Kyiv's position that it was not willing to cede territory to Russia. But he added that if the country reached a comprehensive deal, including security guarantees, a ‌strong ​and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question ​to the public in a referendum.

Recent findings suggest that "That ​is why ⁠I believe NATO is back on the ⁠agenda. ​But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation.".

Zelenskyy said the prospect of NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas has not been raised before.

He also warned about Moscow's plan to  change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.

Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.

"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.

"Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe.".

On Friday, the EU noted several European diplomats would take part in future Ukraine peace talks, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland.

Moscow has long insisted that European states be excluded from the negotiations because they support Ukraine.

The comments come as Russia’s Defence Ministry said its ⁠forces ⁠had captured the ​settlement of Tersianka in ​Ukraine’s southeastern ​Zaporizhzhia ‌region, news agency Interfax reported.

Interfax cited the ministry as saying that Russian ​forces had struck Ukrainian energy and ​transport infrastructure used by ⁠the ​military, along with ammunition ​depots and ​drone production ‌and storage sites.

Russia has targeted power stations across Ukraine in waves of ballistic and cruise missile attacks, cutting power and heating to millions of people as temperatures plunge.

Zelenskyy warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's war campaign, which Kyiv insists is aimed at hurting public morale.

Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that slowing climate change requires overcoming inertia in political, technological and geophysical systems1,2,3.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that slowing climate change requires overcoming inertia in political, technological and geophysical systems1,2,3. Portland cement manufacturing is among the most challenging industrial processes to decarbonize, yet it remains indispensable for building the infrastructure underpinning the low-carbon transition4,5. Here, building beyond the two-century-old conventional cement process6, we report a route that creates sustainable cement, by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds. Our technique generates localized temperatures up to 2,400 °C, sufficient to liquefy the raw materials. These liquid-phase reactions promote elemental mixing and solidification, producing reactive clinker phases. Our in situ transmission electron microscopy captures the early-stage cement hydration process in real time, revealing that surface disorder accelerates clinker reactivity by facilitating the dynamic nucleation and growth of hydration clusters. Beyond typical limestone and clay feedstocks, we show that hydrated cement paste from waste concrete can also be processed into clinkers, meeting ordinary Portland cement specifications. By coupling circular resource use with ultrafast electrified processing, our approach enables sustainable, low-cost cement production at scale.

#117480. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1379 w)
