The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany.
  • This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
  • Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Sources indicate that virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas.".

Industry observers note that support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

It has been revealed that particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it.".

According to recent reports, the debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:.

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

In a recent development, according to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

Industry observers note that the question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

Recent findings suggest that but how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she stated in an interview with DW.

It has been revealed that neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?".

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

It has been revealed that DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

In a recent development, the party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization.".

Virchow notes that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

Recent findings suggest that * Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The 28-year-old Greece international has established himself as one of the most prolific goalscorers in European football, attracting considerable attention from Premier League clubs following his outstanding start to the season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham Hotspur are stepping up their interest in Benfica striker Vangelis Pavlidis as Roberto De Zerbi assesses potential attacking reinforcements ahead of the January transfer window.

The 28-year-old Greece international has established himself as one of the most prolific goalscorers in European football, attracting considerable attention from Premier League clubs following his outstanding start to the season.

Tottenham are now closely monitoring his performances, although convincing Benfica to sanction a mid-season departure could prove difficult.

According to Portuguese publication Record, Tottenham have regularly sent scouts to Benfica matches specifically to assess Pavlidis.

The Greek forward has scored an impressive 19 goals in 20 appearances across all competitions this season, further enhancing his reputation as a reliable goalscorer.

Pavlidis has become an important figure in Benfica’s attack, contributing through his movement, physical presence and ability to involve teammates in attacking moves.

However, Tottenham are not alone in their admiration for the striker.

A recent CaughtOffside report revealed that Manchester United are also interested in securing his services.

Benfica’s negotiating position remains strong, with Pavlidis understood to have a €100million release clause in his contract. There is right now no indication that Tottenham have submitted a formal offer.

Signing Pavlidis would represent an interesting departure from Tottenham’s emphasis on recruiting younger players with significant resale potential.

At 28, the Greek international is already in his prime and would arrive with considerable experience rather than requiring several seasons of development.

His intelligent movement inside the penalty area, finishing ability and willingness to contribute outside the box could make him particularly effective in De Zerbi’s attacking system.

However, Tottenham must be careful about the financial commitment involved.

While Pavlidis has consistently delivered goals in Portugal and previously in the Netherlands, adapting to the intensity of Premier League football would present a fresh challenge.

Spending close to his release clause would represent a substantial gamble, particularly given his age.

If Tottenham can negotiate a considerably lower transfer fee, Pavlidis could prove an excellent addition capable of making an immediate impact.

For now, continuing to assess the striker before committing to an expensive January pursuit appears to be the sensible approach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ruben Amorim warns Olympiacos are ‘aggressive, especially at home’ in the Europa League, but Milan ‘have to do well both in the League and in Europe, it’s the only way to be a good team.’.

It kicks off in Athens on Thursday at 17.45 GMT (18.45 CET).

Injuries are piling up for this trip, with Luka Modric, Strahinja Pavlovic, Francesco Camarda and Davide Bartesaghi joining Ruben Loftus-Cheek, Fikayo Tomori, Matteo Gabbia, Samuel Chukwueze, Alexis Saelemaekers and Pietro Terracciano on the treatment table.

At least Mike Maignan is available again after suspension, and confidence was boosted by a 5-1 Serie A victory over Frosinone.

“It’s a fact that we need to improve in the final third,” stated Amorim in his press conference.

“The only thing we can do is improve our principles. We need to improve on these little things, and that’s the only way I can help my players. Against Olympiacos, it will be a different match than the one against Frosinone, just as it will be different than the one against Cagliari.

“We need to improve, even in our defending. We’ve almost always conceded a goal, so that’s another area we need to improve.”.

Olympiacos are sixth in the Europa League table after amassing 10 points from four games, beating Jagiellonia, Olympique Marseille and Sparta Prague before the 0-0 draw away to Stade Rennais.

Notably, they have conceded only one goal in those four matches.

“They’re a strong team. They’re aggressive, especially at home. I’ve played here twice, and it was tough for me. I know their coach and what he wants to do. They play compact, positive football, 4-3-3, they change a lot, they rotate, they have Jota, a lot of Portuguese players.

Industry observers note that “They’re a strong team, and with their fans there, it’ll be a tough match. Chiquinho is a great talent, but very impulsive. I hope he plays well tomorrow, but I hope he still has a great career ahead of him.”.

The Rossoneri’s form in the Europa League has been little short of disastrous, as the 4-0 victory away to RB Salzburg was an outlier between three defeats to Benfica, Bournemouth and Ferencvaros, all without scoring a single goal.

“To be a good team, you have to do well both in the league and in Europe,” insisted Amorim.

“That’s the only way to be a good team. We have to be, especially at Milan. I’m always waiting for things to go badly, because it doesn’t take much to change the situation. That’s what I’m trying to make my players understand, because it won’t always be this way. We’re at the beginning of a process, and I think we need everyone.

According to recent reports, “We lost Pavlovic, Modric, Saelemaekers, Chukwueze, and everyone has to be ready, because there are no excuses at big clubs. We have to be ready for this. I can’t believe we lost all these games in Europe because we rotated.

“We have to always be ready and approach the games like against Inter, Frosinone, and Genoa. We’re building so many things. Tomorrow is another test for us.”.

Does Amorim still believe that Milan will be able to challenge for the Scudetto?

“I haven’t changed my mind. This year is difficult, but if we have the chance to fight, we’ll do it.”.

Many coaches have been asked about the release of the Grand Theft Auto VI game and how much time players are committing to it.

“I’d rather my players play that every day rather than scroll through social media,” replied Amorim.

“Social media, and all that stuff, is very difficult for players, who in any case live with more criticism than I do. After Frosinone, I haven’t read anything, because that’s how I want to live my life.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 15:52 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 18:32 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • Celtic have revealed a long-term partnership with a firm the club believe will transform their recruitment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 15:52 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 18:32 EST, 25 November 2026.

Celtic have revealed a long-term partnership with a firm the club believe will transform their recruitment.

London-based Pluto Data Analytics use predictive analytics and AI to help football clubs with player identification. The initial deal lasts three years, with scope for extension.

Celtic believe the deal will ‘support the club’s continuing commitment to innovation and excellence in football operations by enhancing recruitment analysis, talent identification, squad planning and broader football decision-making processes.’.

The Parkhead club’s recruitment strategy has been heavily criticised by supporters in recent seasons amid their struggles in Europe and increased domestic competition from Rangers and Hearts.

A statement explaining the arrangement added: ‘The partnership forms part of Celtic’s ongoing investment in modern football infrastructure and its commitment to ensuring that football decisions are informed by the best available intelligence and expertise.

‘By working with Pluto Data Analytics, Celtic will gain access to enhanced analytical tools and insights to support its existing recruitment and football operations functions.

The Parkhead club are hoping that upcoming deal will improve their recruitment process.

‘The objective is clear: to improve decision-making, identify emerging opportunities and support the club’s long-term football strategy.’.

The move comes following long-standing criticism that the Scottish champions’ means of scouting undervalued talents had become outdated, with their failure to act swiftly and efficiently in the transfer market leading to repeated failures in the European qualification rounds.

Rival clubs such as Hearts have benefited from the use of data thanks to the access they have had to Jamestown Analytics.

‘We are always looking for ways to strengthen our football operation and ensure that we continue to evolve in an increasingly competitive environment,’ said Celtic chief executive Michael Nicholson.

‘We have been reviewing the options in this area in order to select the optimum model for our club.

‘Our partnership with Pluto Data Analytics, an organisation with real quality and pedigree within this field, reflects our commitment to innovation and continuous improvement.

O'Neill states he hopes partnership 'will help us deliver the success we are all striving for'.

Industry observers note that ‘Recruitment remains one of the most important areas of any football club. Our aim is to identify talent as effectively as possible, reduce uncertainty where we can and support our football staff with the best available information.

‘We believe this partnership will strengthen our ability to support the club’s ambitions both domestically and in European competition.’.

Manager Martin O’Neill added: ‘I am very pleased that Celtic and Pluto are joining together to give the club an extra level of insight and analysis which is becoming more prominent in football.

‘While football is not an exact science, if the club can access and utilise newly introduced tools and new details, ultimately, we hope that such data will help us deliver the success we are all striving for.

Celtic chief executive Michael Nicholson indicates Pluto deal is 'optimum model' for the club.

‘Our recruitment and wider football operations teams have already engaged with Pluto. Our looks in the short, medium and longer term are being developed and we are confident that our relationship will deliver real tangible benefit to the club over the next few years.’.

Jon Godfrey, CEO of Pluto Data Analytics, said: ‘Today is a big day for Pluto and we are incredibly excited to be working with Celtic, one of the biggest clubs in world football.

‘We believe that predictive data modelling combined with the allure and resources of such a famous institution will allow us to achieve great things in this partnership.

‘Celtic has the capacity to compete at the highest levels of European football and it is an honour and a fantastic challenge to work relentlessly with the club on achieving the exciting goals we have put in place.’.
